Repeat steps 1-6 for each network security group requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For a rule that exists only for database access, delete it:  ``` az network nsg rule delete --resource-group <resource-group> --nsg-name <network-security-group> --name <rule> ```  For a rule that also allows other ports, restrict its source or remove the database ports from its destination ports instead:  ``` az network nsg rule update --resource-group <resource-group> --nsg-name <network-security-group> --name <rule> --source-address-prefixes <trusted-address-range> az network nsg rule update --resource-group <resource-group> --nsg-name <network-security-group> --name <rule> --destination-port-ranges <ports-without-database-ports> ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For a rule that exists only for database access, delete it:  ``` Get-AzNetworkSecurityGroup -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <network-security-group> | Remove-AzNetworkSecurityRuleConfig -Name <rule> | Set-AzNetworkSecurityGroup ```  For a rule that also allows other ports, restrict its source instead, or assign the remaining ports to `DestinationPortRange` the same way:  ``` $nsg = Get-AzNetworkSecurityGroup -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <network-security-group> ($nsg.SecurityRules | Where-Object { $_.Name -eq '<rule>' }).SourceAddressPrefix = [System.String[]]@('<trusted-address-range>') $nsg | Set-AzNetworkSecurityGroup ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Network security groups`. 2. Click the name of a network security group. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Inbound security rules`. 4. Ensure that no inbound security rule exists that matches the following: - Port: `1433`, `1434`, `1521`, `3306`, `5432`, `6379`, `27017`, `Any`, or a range including any of these ports - Protocol: `TCP`, `UDP`, or `Any` - Source: `0.0.0.0/0`, `::/0`, `Internet`, or `Any` - Action: `Allow` 5. Repeat steps 1-4 for each network security group.  To audit from Azure Resource Graph:  1. Go to `Resource Graph Explorer`. 2. Click `New query`. 3. Paste the following into the query window:  ``` resources | where type =~ "microsoft.network/networksecuritygroups" | project id, name, securityRule = properties.securityRules | mv-expand securityRule limit 1000 | extend access = securityRule.properties.access, direction = securityRule.properties.direction, protocol = securityRule.properties.protocol, destinationPort = case(isempty(securityRule.properties.destinationPortRange), securityRule.properties.destinationPortRanges, securityRule.properties.destinationPortRange), sourceAddress = case(isempty(securityRule.properties.sourceAddressPrefix), securityRule.properties.sourceAddressPrefixes, securityRule.properties.sourceAddressPrefix) | where access =~ "Allow" and direction =~ "Inbound" and protocol in~ ("tcp", "udp", "*") | mv-expand destinationPort | mv-expand sourceAddress | extend destinationPort = tostring(destinationPort) | extend destinationPortMin = toint(split(destinationPort, "-")[0]), destinationPortMax = toint(split(destinationPort, "-")[-1]) | where destinationPort in ("*", "") or (destinationPortMin <= 1433 and destinationPortMax >= 1433) or (destinationPortMin <= 1434 and destinationPortMax >= 1434) or (destinationPortMin <= 1521 and destinationPortMax >= 1521) or (destinationPortMin <= 3306 and destinationPortMax >= 3306) or (destinationPortMin <= 5432 and destinationPortMax >= 5432) or (destinationPortMin <= 6379 and destinationPortMax >= 6379) or (destinationPortMin <= 27017 and destinationPortMax >= 27017) | where sourceAddress in~ ("*", "0.0.0.0", "internet", "any") or sourceAddress endswith "/0" ```  4. Click `Run query`. 5. Ensure that no results are returned.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  List network security groups with non-default security rules:  ``` az network nsg list --query "[*].[name,securityRules]" ```  Ensure that no network security group has an inbound security rule that matches the following:  ``` "access" : "Allow" "destinationPortRange" : "1433", "1434", "1521", "3306", "5432", "6379", "27017", "*", or "<range-including-one-of-these-ports>" "direction" : "Inbound" "protocol" : "Tcp", "Udp", or "*" "sourceAddressPrefix" : "0.0.0.0/0", "::/0", "Internet", or "*" ```  Check each entry of `destinationPortRanges` and `sourceAddressPrefixes` the same way.  **Audit from PowerShell**  List inbound `Allow` rules for TCP, UDP, or any protocol:  ``` Get-AzNetworkSecurityGroup | ForEach-Object { $nsg = $_ $nsg.SecurityRules | Where-Object { $_.Direction -eq 'Inbound' -and $_.Access -eq 'Allow' -and $_.Protocol -in 'Tcp', 'Udp', '*' } | Select-Object @{n='NetworkSecurityGroup'; e={$nsg.Name}}, @{n='ResourceGroup'; e={$nsg.ResourceGroupName}}, Name, DestinationPortRange, SourceAddressPrefix } ```  Ensure no listed rule pairs a `DestinationPortRange` entry of `1433`, `1434`, `1521`, `3306`, `5432`, `6379`, `27017`, `*`, or a range including one of them with a `SourceAddressPrefix` entry of `0.0.0.0/0`, `::/0`, `Internet`, or `*`.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [9daedab3-fb2d-461e-b861-71790eead4f6](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2F9daedab3-fb2d-461e-b861-71790eead4f6) **- Name:** 'All network ports should be restricted on network security groups associated to your virtual machine'  This definition flags inbound rules from `Any` or `Internet` on any port for network security groups associated with virtual machines, so it also reports exposures other than database ports.
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: The ports are the defaults for SQL Server (1433, and 1434 for the SQL Server Browser service and the dedicated administrator connection), Oracle Database (1521), MySQL (3306), PostgreSQL (5432), Redis (6379), and MongoDB (27017). An engine can listen on any port, and SQL Server named instances use dynamic ports, so identify the port each engine uses and evaluate it the same way. Choosing `Public` SQL connectivity when creating a SQL Server virtual machine in the Azure portal adds a rule that allows the SQL Server port.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, a network security group has no inbound rule allowing database ports from the Internet; the default `DenyAllInBound` rule blocks them.

Requirements.Description: Ensure 'HTTP2' is Set to 'Enabled' on Azure Application Gateway

Attributes.Description: Enable HTTP/2 for improved performance, efficiency, and security.  HTTP/2 protocol support is available to clients that connect to application gateway listeners only. Communication with backend server pools is always HTTP/1.1.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Enabling HTTP/2 supports use of modern encrypted connections.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Clients and backend services that do not support HTTP/2 will fall back to HTTP/1.1.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Application gateways`. 2. Click the name of an application gateway. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Configuration`. 4. Under `HTTP2`, click `Enabled`. 5. Click `Save`. 6. Repeat steps 1-5 for each application gateway requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each application gateway requiring remediation, run the following command to enable HTTP2:  ``` az network application-gateway update --resource-group <resource-group> --name <application-gateway> --http2 Enabled ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  Run the following command to get the application gateway in a resource group with a given name:  ``` $gateway = Get-AzApplicationGateway -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <application-gateway> ```  Run the following command to enable HTTP2:  ``` $gateway.EnableHttp2 = $true ```  Run the following command to apply the update:  ``` Set-AzApplicationGateway -ApplicationGateway $gateway ```  Repeat for each application gateway requiring remediation.
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Application gateways`. 2. Click the name of an application gateway. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Configuration`. 4. Ensure `HTTP2` is set to `Enabled`. 5. Repeat steps 1-4 for each application gateway.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list application gateways:  ``` az network application-gateway list ```  For each application gateway, run the following command to get the HTTP2 setting:  ``` az network application-gateway show --resource-group <resource-group> --name <application-gateway> --query enableHttp2 ```  Ensure `true` is returned.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Run the following command to list application gateways:  ``` Get-AzApplicationGateway ```  Run the following command to get the application gateway in a resource group with a given name:  ``` $gateway = Get-AzApplicationGateway -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <application-gateway> ```  Run the following command to get the HTTP2 setting:  ``` $gateway.EnableHttp2 ```  Ensure `True` is returned.  Repeat for each application gateway.
Attributes.DefaultValue: HTTP2 is enabled by default.

Requirements.Description: Ensure the SSL Policy's 'Min protocol version' is Set to 'TLSv1_2' or Higher on Azure Application Gateway

Attributes.Description: Azure Application Gateway sets the minimum TLS version for client connections through its SSL policy, at the gateway and in each SSL profile. The `Min protocol version` selects `TLSv1_0`, `TLSv1_1`, `TLSv1_2`, or `TLSv1_3`; Microsoft no longer supports TLS 1.0 or 1.1, but a gateway can carry policies that allow them.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: In NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2, NIST has mandated that servers that support both government-only applications as well as citizen or business-facing applications "**shall** be configured to use [or negotiate] TLS 1.2 and **should** be configured to use [or negotiate] TLS 1.3 as well." Further, NIST specifies that "agencies **shall** support TLS 1.3 by January 1, 2024 [for both government-only and citizen or business-facing applications]." In general, NIST indicates that "servers that support TLS 1.3 **should** be configured to use TLS 1.2 as well. However, TLS 1.2 may be disabled on servers that support TLS 1.3 [if TLS 1.2 is not needed for interoperability]."  **POST-QUANTUM CRYPTOGRAPHY:** TLS v1.3 introduces cryptographic suites which make Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) algorithms accessible. Where possible, TLS v1.3 should be implemented as the sole protocol in use for the security of data in transit, but only if TLS 1.2 interoperability is not required.  These protocols are outdated, vulnerable, and **shall not** be used: TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, SSL 2.0, SSL 3.0.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Clients limited to TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 cannot connect. The SSL policy does not affect backend connections. Legacy policies cannot coexist with 2022 predefined or `CustomV2` policies on one gateway, so moving the gateway to a 2022 policy can require changing every SSL profile in the same update.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Note:** The PowerShell method updates the gateway and its SSL profiles in one operation, which avoids a failed update when an SSL profile still carries a legacy policy.  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Navigate to `Application gateways`. 2. Click the name of an application gateway. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Listeners`. 4. Under `SSL Policy`, next to the `Selected SSL Policy` name, click `change`. 5. Select `Predefined`. 6. Select `AppGwSslPolicy20220101S`, or another policy with a `Min protocol version` of `TLSv1_2` or higher. 7. Click `Save`. 8. Under `Settings`, click `SSL settings`. 9. Click the name of an SSL profile. 10. Click the `SSL Policy` tab. 11. If `Enable listener-specific SSL Policy` is checked, select `Predefined`. 12. Select `AppGwSslPolicy20220101S`, or another policy with a `Min protocol version` of `TLSv1_2` or higher. 13. Click `Save`. 14. Repeat steps 9-13 for each SSL profile. 15. Repeat steps 1-14 for each application gateway requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each application gateway requiring remediation, set the gateway SSL policy:  ``` az network application-gateway ssl-policy set --resource-group <resource-group> --gateway-name <application-gateway> --policy-type Predefined --name AppGwSslPolicy20220101S ```  For each SSL profile with a listener-specific SSL policy, set its policy:  ``` az network application-gateway ssl-profile update --resource-group <resource-group> --gateway-name <application-gateway> --name <ssl-profile> --policy-type Predefined --policy-name AppGwSslPolicy20220101S ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each application gateway requiring remediation, update the gateway and SSL profile policies:  ``` $gw = Get-AzApplicationGateway -ResourceGroupName "<resource-group>" -Name "<application-gateway>" Set-AzApplicationGatewaySslPolicy -ApplicationGateway $gw -PolicyType Predefined -PolicyName AppGwSslPolicy20220101S foreach ($p in $gw.SslProfiles | Where-Object { $_.SslPolicy }) { Set-AzApplicationGatewaySslProfilePolicy -SslProfile $p -PolicyType Predefined -PolicyName AppGwSslPolicy20220101S } Set-AzApplicationGateway -ApplicationGateway $gw ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Navigate to `Application gateways`. 2. Click the name of an application gateway. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Listeners`. 4. Under `SSL Policy`, ensure `Min protocol version` is `TLSv1_2` or `TLSv1_3`. 5. Under `Settings`, click `SSL settings`. 6. Click the name of an SSL profile. 7. Click the `SSL Policy` tab. 8. If `Enable listener-specific SSL Policy` is checked, ensure `Min protocol version` is `TLSv1_2` or `TLSv1_3`. 9. Repeat steps 6-8 for each SSL profile. 10. Repeat steps 1-9 for each application gateway.  A `Min protocol version` of `TLSv1_0` or `TLSv1_1` is non-compliant.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  List the SSL policies of every gateway and SSL profile:  ``` az network application-gateway list --query "[].{name:name, policyType:sslPolicy.policyType, policyName:sslPolicy.policyName, minProtocolVersion:sslPolicy.minProtocolVersion, sslProfiles:sslProfiles[].{name:name, policyType:sslPolicy.policyType, policyName:sslPolicy.policyName, minProtocolVersion:sslPolicy.minProtocolVersion}}" ```  Any `minProtocolVersion` of `TLSv1_0` or `TLSv1_1`, or `policyName` of `AppGwSslPolicy20150501` or `AppGwSslPolicy20170401`, is non-compliant. Any other result is compliant; an empty gateway policy uses the default.  **Audit from PowerShell**  List the SSL policies of every gateway and SSL profile:  ``` Get-AzApplicationGateway | ForEach-Object { $gw = $_ [pscustomobject]@{ Gateway = $gw.Name; Scope = 'Gateway'; PolicyType = $gw.SslPolicy.PolicyType; PolicyName = $gw.SslPolicy.PolicyName; MinProtocolVersion = $gw.SslPolicy.MinProtocolVersion } foreach ($p in $gw.SslProfiles) { [pscustomobject]@{ Gateway = $gw.Name; Scope = $p.Name; PolicyType = $p.SslPolicy.PolicyType; PolicyName = $p.SslPolicy.PolicyName; MinProtocolVersion = $p.SslPolicy.MinProtocolVersion } } } | Format-Table ```  Any `MinProtocolVersion` of `TLSv1_0` or `TLSv1_1`, or `PolicyName` of `AppGwSslPolicy20150501` or `AppGwSslPolicy20170401`, is non-compliant. Any other result is compliant.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [6313cbe8-6fb7-451b-a9e3-3f23b59843ca](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2F6313cbe8-6fb7-451b-a9e3-3f23b59843ca) **- Name:** 'Azure Application Gateway should be running TLS version 1.2 or newer' [Preview]
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: The predefined policies with a `TLSv1_2` minimum are `AppGwSslPolicy20170401S`, `AppGwSslPolicy20220101`, and `AppGwSslPolicy20220101S`; only the 2022 policies also enable TLS 1.3. Post-quantum key exchange, such as the hybrid ML-KEM groups, is defined only for TLS 1.3, and TLS 1.2 cannot negotiate it, so a TLS 1.3 minimum is the prerequisite for post-quantum protection. As of October 27, 2026, Application Gateway documents no post-quantum key exchange support. To refuse TLS 1.2, see the Level 2 recommendation `Ensure the SSL Policy's 'Min protocol version' is Set to 'TLSv1_3' on Azure Application Gateway`.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, a gateway with no SSL policy set uses `AppGwSslPolicy20220101`, whose minimum protocol version is `TLSv1_2`.

Requirements.Description: Ensure the SSL Policy's 'Min protocol version' is Set to 'TLSv1_3' on Azure Application Gateway

Attributes.Description: Azure Application Gateway sets the minimum TLS version for client connections through its SSL policy, at the gateway and in each SSL profile. The `Min protocol version` selects `TLSv1_2` or `TLSv1_3` on a supported policy, and only a `CustomV2` policy can select `TLSv1_3`.  **Prerequisites:** Confirm from the gateway's `Client TLS protocol` metric that no client that must keep access still connects with TLS 1.2.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: With TLS 1.2 enabled, the gateway's policy can permit cipher suites without forward secrecy, and TLS 1.2 handshakes send the server certificate unencrypted. If the certificate's private key is later exposed, traffic recorded under those suites can be decrypted. NIST SP 800-52 Revision 2 permits disabling TLS 1.2 on servers that support TLS 1.3 when interoperability does not require it.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Clients that cannot negotiate TLS 1.3, such as older operating systems, runtimes, and embedded devices, fail the handshake. The SSL policy does not affect backend connections. Listeners that share a port must use the same minimum version, so an exception for TLS 1.2 clients requires a separate port and a separate SSL profile.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Note:** The PowerShell method updates the gateway and its SSL profiles in one operation, which avoids a failed update when an SSL profile still carries a legacy policy.  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Navigate to `Application gateways`. 2. Click the name of an application gateway. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Listeners`. 4. Under `SSL Policy`, next to the `Selected SSL Policy` name, click `change`. 5. Select `CustomV2`. 6. Select `TLSv1_3` for `Min protocol version`. 7. Click `Save`. 8. Under `Settings`, click `SSL settings`. 9. Click the name of an SSL profile. 10. Click the `SSL Policy` tab. 11. If `Enable listener-specific SSL Policy` is checked, select `CustomV2`. 12. Select `TLSv1_3` for `Min protocol version`. 13. Click `Save`. 14. Repeat steps 9-13 for each SSL profile. 15. Repeat steps 1-14 for each application gateway requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each application gateway requiring remediation, set the gateway SSL policy:  ``` az network application-gateway ssl-policy set --resource-group <resource-group> --gateway-name <application-gateway> --policy-type CustomV2 --min-protocol-version TLSv1_3 ```  For each SSL profile with a listener-specific SSL policy, set its policy:  ``` az network application-gateway ssl-profile update --resource-group <resource-group> --gateway-name <application-gateway> --name <ssl-profile> --policy-type CustomV2 --min-protocol-version TLSv1_3 ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each application gateway requiring remediation, update the gateway and SSL profile policies:  ``` $gw = Get-AzApplicationGateway -ResourceGroupName "<resource-group>" -Name "<application-gateway>" Set-AzApplicationGatewaySslPolicy -ApplicationGateway $gw -PolicyType CustomV2 -MinProtocolVersion TLSv1_3 -CipherSuite @() foreach ($p in $gw.SslProfiles | Where-Object { $_.SslPolicy }) { Set-AzApplicationGatewaySslProfilePolicy -SslProfile $p -PolicyType CustomV2 -MinProtocolVersion TLSv1_3 -CipherSuite @() } Set-AzApplicationGateway -ApplicationGateway $gw ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Navigate to `Application gateways`. 2. Click the name of an application gateway. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Listeners`. 4. Under `SSL Policy`, ensure `Min protocol version` is `TLSv1_3`. 5. Under `Settings`, click `SSL settings`. 6. Click the name of an SSL profile. 7. Click the `SSL Policy` tab. 8. If `Enable listener-specific SSL Policy` is checked, ensure `Min protocol version` is `TLSv1_3`. 9. Repeat steps 6-8 for each SSL profile. 10. Repeat steps 1-9 for each application gateway.  Any other `Min protocol version` is non-compliant.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  List the SSL policies of every gateway and SSL profile:  ``` az network application-gateway list --query "[].{name:name, policyType:sslPolicy.policyType, policyName:sslPolicy.policyName, minProtocolVersion:sslPolicy.minProtocolVersion, sslProfiles:sslProfiles[].{name:name, policyType:sslPolicy.policyType, policyName:sslPolicy.policyName, minProtocolVersion:sslPolicy.minProtocolVersion}}" ```  Each gateway, and each SSL profile with policy values, must return `minProtocolVersion` `TLSv1_3`; a profile without values inherits the gateway policy. Any other result is non-compliant.  **Audit from PowerShell**  List the SSL policies of every gateway and SSL profile:  ``` Get-AzApplicationGateway | ForEach-Object { $gw = $_ [pscustomobject]@{ Gateway = $gw.Name; Scope = 'Gateway'; PolicyType = $gw.SslPolicy.PolicyType; PolicyName = $gw.SslPolicy.PolicyName; MinProtocolVersion = $gw.SslPolicy.MinProtocolVersion } foreach ($p in $gw.SslProfiles) { [pscustomobject]@{ Gateway = $gw.Name; Scope = $p.Name; PolicyType = $p.SslPolicy.PolicyType; PolicyName = $p.SslPolicy.PolicyName; MinProtocolVersion = $p.SslPolicy.MinProtocolVersion } } } | Format-Table ```  The `Gateway` scope row, and each SSL profile row with values, must show `MinProtocolVersion` `TLSv1_3`; a profile row without values inherits the gateway policy. Any other result is non-compliant.
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: Only a `CustomV2` policy sets a TLS 1.3 minimum; it enables `TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384` and `TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256`, which CLI and PowerShell output omit. Post-quantum key exchange, such as the hybrid ML-KEM groups, is defined only for TLS 1.3, and TLS 1.2 cannot negotiate it, so a TLS 1.3 minimum is the prerequisite for post-quantum protection. As of October 27, 2026, Application Gateway documents no post-quantum key exchange support. It extends the Level 1 recommendation `Ensure the SSL Policy's 'Min protocol version' is Set to 'TLSv1_2' or Higher on Azure Application Gateway`.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, a gateway with no SSL policy set uses `AppGwSslPolicy20220101`, whose minimum protocol version is `TLSv1_2`.

Requirements.Description: Ensure Bot Protection is Enabled in Azure Web Application Firewall Policy on Azure Application Gateway

Attributes.Description: Enable bot protection on the Web Application Firewall to block or log requests from known malicious IP addresses identified through the Microsoft Threat Intelligence feed.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Internet traffic from bots can scrape, scan, and search for application vulnerabilities. Enabling bot protection stops requests from known malicious IP addresses and enhances the overall security of your application by reducing exposure to automated attacks.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: May require monitoring to identify false positives.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Application gateways`. 2. Click the name of an application gateway. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Web application firewall`. 4. Under `Associated web application firewall policy`, click the policy name. 5. Under `Settings`, click `Managed rules`. 6. Click `Assign`. 7. Under `Bot Management ruleset`, click to display the drop-down menu. 8. Select a `Microsoft_BotManagerRuleSet`. 9. Click `Save`. 10. Click `X` to close the panel. 11. Repeat steps 1-10 for each application gateway and firewall policy requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each firewall policy requiring remediation, run the following command to enable bot protection:  ``` az network application-gateway waf-policy managed-rule rule-set add --resource-group <resource-group> --policy-name <firewall-policy> --type Microsoft_BotManagerRuleSet --version <0.1|1.0|1.1> ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Application gateways`. 2. Click the name of an application gateway. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Web application firewall`. 4. Under `Associated web application firewall policy`, click the policy name. 5. Under `Settings`, click `Managed rules`. 6. Ensure a `Rule Id` containing `Microsoft_BotManagerRuleSet` is listed. 7. Click the `>` to expand the row. 8. Ensure the `Status` for `Malicious Bots` is set to `Enabled`. 9. Repeat steps 1-8 for each application gateway.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list application gateways:  ``` az network application-gateway list ```  For each application gateway, run the following command to get the firewall policy id:  ``` az network application-gateway show --resource-group <resource-group> --name <application-gateway> --query firewallPolicy.id ```  For each firewall policy, run the following command to get the managed rule sets:  ``` az network application-gateway waf-policy show --ids <firewall-policy> --query managedRules.managedRuleSets ```  Ensure a managed rule set with `ruleSetType` of `Microsoft_BotManagerRuleSet` is returned, and that no `ruleGroupOverrides` for `ruleGroupName` `KnownBadBots` with `state` `Disabled` are returned.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [ebea0d86-7fbd-42e3-8a46-27e7568c2525](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2Febea0d86-7fbd-42e3-8a46-27e7568c2525) **- Name:** 'Bot Protection should be enabled for Azure Application Gateway WAF'
Attributes.DefaultValue: Bot protection is disabled by default on Azure Application Gateways with Web Application Firewall.

Requirements.Description: Ensure Request Body Inspection is Enabled in Azure Web Application Firewall policy on Azure Application Gateway

Attributes.Description: Enable request body inspection so that the Web Application Firewall evaluates the contents of HTTP message bodies for potential threats.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Enabling request body inspection strengthens security by allowing the Web Application Firewall to detect common attacks, such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Minor performance impact on the Web Application Firewall. Additional effort may be required to monitor findings.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Application gateways`. 2. Click the name of an application gateway. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Web application firewall`. 4. Under `Associated web application firewall policy`, click the policy name. 5. Under `Settings`, click `Policy settings`. 6. Check the box next to `Enforce request body inspection`. 7. Click `Save`. 8. Repeat steps 1-7 for each application gateway and firewall policy requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each firewall policy requiring remediation, run the following command to enable request body inspection:  ``` az network application-gateway waf-policy update --ids <firewall-policy> --policy-settings request-body-check=true ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Application gateways`. 2. Click the name of an application gateway. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Web application firewall`. 4. Under `Associated web application firewall policy`, click the policy name. 5. Under `Settings`, click `Policy settings`. 6. Ensure the box next to `Enforce request body inspection` is checked. 7. Repeat steps 1-6 for each application gateway.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list application gateways:  ``` az network application-gateway list ```  For each application gateway, run the following command to get the firewall policy id:  ``` az network application-gateway show --resource-group <resource-group> --name <application-gateway> --query firewallPolicy.id ```  For each firewall policy, run the following command to get the request body inspection setting:  ``` az network application-gateway waf-policy show --ids <firewall-policy> --query policySettings.requestBodyCheck ```  Ensure `true` is returned.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [ca85ef9a-741d-461d-8b7a-18c2da82c666](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2Fca85ef9a-741d-461d-8b7a-18c2da82c666) **- Name:** 'Azure Web Application Firewall on Azure Application Gateway should have request body inspection enabled'
Attributes.DefaultValue: Request body inspection is enabled by default on Azure Application Gateways with Web Application Firewall.

Requirements.Description: Ensure Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) is Enabled on Azure Application Gateway

Attributes.Description: Azure Web Application Firewall helps protect applications from common exploits and attacks by inspecting and filtering incoming traffic.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Using Azure Web Application Firewall with Azure Application Gateway reduces exposure to external threats by mitigating attacks on public facing applications.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: The `WAF V2` tier for Azure Application Gateways costs more than the `Basic` and `Standard V2` tiers. Pricing includes a fixed hourly charge plus a charge per capacity-unit hour. Refer to https://azure.microsoft.com/en-gb/pricing/details/application-gateway/ for details.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Note:** `Basic` tier application gateways cannot be upgraded to the `WAF V2` tier. Create a new `WAF V2` tier application gateway to replace a `Basic` tier application gateway.  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  To remediate a `Standard V2` tier application gateway:  1. Go to `Application gateways`. 2. Click `Add filter`. 3. From the `Filter` drop-down menu, select `SKU size`. 4. Check the box next to `Standard_v2` only. 5. Click `Apply`. 6. Click the name of an application gateway. 7. Under `Settings`, click `Web application firewall`. 8. Under `Configure`, next to `Tier`, click `WAF V2`. 9. Select an existing or create a new `WAF policy`. 10. Click `Save`. 11. Repeat steps 1-10 for each `Standard V2` tier application gateway requiring remediation.
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Application gateways`. 2. Click the name of an application gateway. 3. In the `Overview`, under `Essentials`, ensure `Tier` is set to `WAF V2`. 4. Repeat steps 1-3 for each application gateway.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list application gateways:  ``` az network application-gateway list ```  For each application gateway, run the following command to get the firewall policy id:  ``` az network application-gateway show --resource-group <resource-group> --name <application-gateway> --query firewallPolicy.id ```  Ensure a firewall policy id is returned.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [564feb30-bf6a-4854-b4bb-0d2d2d1e6c66](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2F564feb30-bf6a-4854-b4bb-0d2d2d1e6c66) **- Name:** 'Web Application Firewall (WAF) should be enabled for Application Gateway'
Attributes.DefaultValue: Azure Web Application Firewall is enabled by default for the `WAF V2` tier of Azure Application Gateway. It is not available in the `Basic` tier. Application gateways deployed using the `Standard V2` tier can be upgraded to the `WAF V2` tier to enable Azure Web Application Firewall.

Requirements.Description: Ensure that Public IP Addresses are Evaluated on a Periodic Basis

Attributes.Description: Public IP Addresses provide tenant accounts with Internet connectivity for resources contained within the tenant. During the creation of certain resources in Azure, a Public IP Address may be created. All Public IP Addresses within the tenant should be periodically reviewed for accuracy and necessity.  While an automated assessment procedure exists for this recommendation, the assessment status remains manual. Evaluating the appropriateness of public IP addresses requires a manual review, as it depends on the specific needs and context of each organization and environment.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Public IP Addresses allocated to the tenant should be periodically reviewed for necessity. Public IP Addresses that are not intentionally assigned and controlled present a publicly facing vector for threat actors and significant risk to the tenant.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: Remediation will vary significantly depending on your organization's security requirements for the resources attached to each individual Public IP address.
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Open the `All Resources` blade 2. Click on `Add Filter` 3. In the Add Filter window, select the following: Filter: `Type` Operator: `Equals` Value: `Public IP address` 4. Click the `Apply` button 5. For each Public IP address in the list, use Overview (or Properties) to review the `"Associated to:"` field and determine if the associated resource is still relevant to your tenant environment. If the associated resource is relevant, ensure that additional controls exist to mitigate risk (e.g. Firewalls, VPNs, Traffic Filtering, Virtual Gateway Appliances, Web Application Firewalls, etc.) on all subsequently attached resources.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  List all Public IP addresses:  ``` az network public-ip list ```  For each Public IP address in the output, review the `"name"` property and determine if the associated resource is still relevant to your tenant environment. If the associated resource is relevant, ensure that additional controls exist to mitigate risk (e.g. Firewalls, VPNs, Traffic Filtering, Virtual Gateway Appliances, Web Application Firewalls, etc.) on all subsequently attached resources.
Attributes.DefaultValue: During Virtual Machine and Application creation, a setting may create and attach a public IP.

Requirements.Description: Ensure Subnets Are Associated with Network Security Groups

Attributes.Description: Each subnet must have an associated network security group to filter its traffic; an unassociated subnet's `Network security group` setting shows `None`. `GatewaySubnet`, `AzureFirewallSubnet`, and `RouteServerSubnet` do not support a network security group, and Microsoft reserves `AzureFirewallManagementSubnet` for the firewall's management traffic, so all four are out of scope.  **Prerequisites:** (Only if using Azure Bastion) Before associating a network security group with `AzureBastionSubnet`, add every inbound and outbound rule Azure Bastion requires; Azure rejects the association otherwise, and a later deny rule that shadows them breaks Bastion connections.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Unprotected subnets can expose resources to unauthorized access.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Minor administrative effort is required to ensure subnets are associated with network security groups. There is no cost to create or use network security groups.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: If using Azure Bastion, complete the prerequisites in the Description before associating a network security group with `AzureBastionSubnet`.  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Virtual networks`. 2. Click the name of a virtual network. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Subnets`. 4. Click the name of a subnet requiring remediation. 5. Under `Security`, next to `Network security group`, click `None` to display the drop-down menu. 6. Select a network security group. 7. Click `Save`. 8. Repeat steps 1-7 for each virtual network and subnet requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each subnet requiring remediation, run the following command to associate it with a network security group:  ``` az network vnet subnet update --resource-group <resource-group> --vnet-name <virtual-network> --name <subnet> --network-security-group <network-security-group> ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Virtual networks`. 2. Click the name of a virtual network. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Subnets`. 4. Click the name of a subnet other than `GatewaySubnet`, `AzureFirewallSubnet`, `AzureFirewallManagementSubnet`, or `RouteServerSubnet`. 5. Under `Security`, ensure `Network security group` is not set to `None`. 6. Repeat steps 1-5 for each virtual network and subnet.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command:  ``` az network vnet list --query "[].{resourceGroup:resourceGroup, virtualNetwork:name, subnets:subnets[?name!='GatewaySubnet' && name!='AzureFirewallSubnet' && name!='AzureFirewallManagementSubnet' && name!='RouteServerSubnet'].{subnet:name, networkSecurityGroup:networkSecurityGroup.id}}" --output json ```  Ensure that every listed subnet has a `networkSecurityGroup` value.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [e71308d3-144b-4262-b144-efdc3cc90517](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2Fe71308d3-144b-4262-b144-efdc3cc90517) **- Name:** 'Subnets should be associated with a Network Security Group'  This Policy reads the Microsoft Defender for Cloud recommendation 'Subnets should be associated with a network security group', which is disabled by default; enable it in the Defender for Cloud security policy before relying on the results. Defender reports `GatewaySubnet`, `AzureFirewallSubnet`, and `AzureBastionSubnet` as not applicable, which the Policy counts as compliant, so check `AzureBastionSubnet` with the Azure Portal or Azure CLI method, and treat any `RouteServerSubnet` or `AzureFirewallManagementSubnet` result as out of scope.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, a subnet is not associated with a network security group.

Requirements.Description: Ensure that Network Watcher is 'Enabled' for Azure Regions That are in Use

Attributes.Description: Enable Network Watcher for physical regions in Azure subscriptions.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Network diagnostic and visualization tools available with Network Watcher help users understand, diagnose, and gain insights to the network in Azure.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: There are additional costs per transaction to run and store network data. For high-volume networks these charges will add up quickly.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: Opting out of Network Watcher automatic enablement is a permanent change. Once you opt-out you cannot opt-in without contacting support.  To manually enable Network Watcher in each region where you want to use Network Watcher capabilities, follow the steps below.  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Use the Search bar to search for and click on the `Network Watcher` service. 2. Click `Create`. 3. Select a `Region` from the drop-down menu. 4. Click `Add`.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  ``` az network watcher configure --locations <region> --enabled true --resource-group <resource_group> ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Use the Search bar to search for and click on the `Network Watcher` service. 2. From the Overview menu item, review each Network Watcher listed, and ensure that a network watcher is listed for each region in use by the subscription.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  ``` az network watcher list --query "[].{Location:location,State:provisioningState}" -o table ```  This will list all network watchers and their provisioning state. Ensure `provisioningState` is `Succeeded` for each network watcher.  ``` az account list-locations --query "[?metadata.regionType=='Physical'].{Name:name,DisplayName:regionalDisplayName}" -o table ```  This will list all physical regions that exist in the subscription. Compare this list to the previous one to ensure that for each region in use, a network watcher exists with `provisioningState` set to `Succeeded`.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Get a list of Network Watchers  ``` Get-AzNetworkWatcher ```  Make sure each watcher is set with the `ProvisioningState` setting set to `Succeeded` and all `Locations` that are in use by the subscription are using a watcher.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [b6e2945c-0b7b-40f5-9233-7a5323b5cdc6](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2Fb6e2945c-0b7b-40f5-9233-7a5323b5cdc6) **- Name:** 'Network Watcher should be enabled'
Attributes.DefaultValue: Network Watcher is automatically enabled. When you create or update a virtual network in your subscription, Network Watcher will be enabled automatically in your Virtual Network's region. There is no impact to your resources or associated charge for automatically enabling Network Watcher.

Requirements.Description: Ensure that Virtual Network Flow Log Retention Days is Set to Greater than or Equal to 90

Attributes.Description: Ensure that virtual network flow logs are retained for greater than or equal to 90 days.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Virtual network flow logs provide critical visibility into traffic patterns. Logs can be used to check for anomalies and give insight into suspected breaches.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: - Virtual network flow logs are charged per gigabyte of network flow logs collected and come with a free tier of 5 GB/month per subscription. - If traffic analytics is enabled with virtual network flow logs, traffic analytics pricing applies at per gigabyte processing rates. - The storage of logs is charged separately, and the cost will depend on the amount of logs and the retention period.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Network Watcher`. 2. Under `Logs`, select `Flow logs`. 3. Click `Add filter`. 4. From the `Filter` drop-down menu, select `Flow log type`. 5. From the `Value` drop-down menu, check `Virtual network` only. 6. Click `Apply`. 7. Click the name of a virtual network flow log. 8. Under `Storage Account`, set `Retention days` to `0`, `90`, or a number greater than 90. If `Retention days` is set to `0`, the logs are retained indefinitely with no retention policy. 9. Repeat steps 7 and 8 for each virtual network flow log requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  Run the following command update the retention policy for a flow log in a network watcher, setting `retention` to `0`, `90`, or a number greater than 90:  ``` az network watcher flow-log update --location <location> --name <flow-log> --retention <number-of-days> ```  Repeat for each virtual network flow log requiring remediation.
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Network Watcher`. 2. Under `Logs`, select `Flow logs`. 3. Click `Add filter`. 4. From the `Filter` drop-down menu, select `Flow log type`. 5. From the `Value` drop-down menu, check `Virtual network` only. 6. Click `Apply`. 7. Click the name of a virtual network flow log. 8. Under `Storage Account`, ensure that `Retention days` is set to `0`, `90`, or a number greater than 90. If `Retention days` is set to `0`, the logs are retained indefinitely with no retention policy. 9. Repeat steps 7 and 8 for each virtual network flow log.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list network watchers:  ``` az network watcher list ```  Run the following command to list the name and retention policy of flow logs in a network watcher:  ``` az network watcher flow-log list --location <location> --query [*].[name,retentionPolicy] ```  For each flow log, ensure that `days` is set to `0`, `90`, or a number greater than 90. If `days` is set to `0`, the logs are retained indefinitely with no retention policy.  Repeat for each network watcher.
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: As network security group flow logs are on the retirement path, Azure recommends migrating to virtual network flow logs.
Attributes.DefaultValue: When a virtual network flow log is created using the Azure CLI, retention days is set to 0 by default. When creating via the Azure Portal, retention days must be specified by the creator.

Requirements.Description: Ensure 'Authentication type' is Set to 'Microsoft Entra ID' Only for Azure VPN Gateway Point-to-Site Configuration

Attributes.Description: Azure VPN Gateway point-to-site connections authenticate clients with any combination of `Azure certificate`, `RADIUS authentication`, and `Microsoft Entra ID`. The `Authentication type` setting selects which of these methods the gateway accepts.  **Prerequisites:** Before removing certificate or RADIUS authentication, add Microsoft Entra ID alongside it and deploy the Azure VPN Client profile to every point-to-site user, as the first remediation step describes.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Client certificates and RADIUS credentials sit outside the organization's identity provider: a certificate is a long-lived file that works from any device holding it, and RADIUS relies on a separate credential store. A stolen certificate or RADIUS credential grants access to the virtual network with no Conditional Access, multifactor authentication, or central revocation.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Microsoft Entra ID authentication works only over OpenVPN and only with the Azure VPN Client for Windows and macOS; the Linux client retired on August 31, 2026. Linux, IKEv2, and SSTP clients lose access once the other methods are removed. SSTP cannot be combined with OpenVPN, and the gateway cannot use the Basic SKU or a policy-based VPN type.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Note:** The `Audience` value below is the Microsoft-registered Azure VPN Client app ID; substitute a custom audience app ID if the organization registered one.  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Virtual network gateways`. 2. Click the name of a VPN gateway. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Point-to-site configuration`. 4. Set `Tunnel type` to a value that includes `OpenVPN (SSL)`. 5. In `Authentication type`, select `Microsoft Entra ID` in addition to the existing selection. 6. Set `Tenant` to `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>`, `Audience` to `c632b3df-fb67-4d84-bdcf-b95ad541b5c8`, and `Issuer` to `https://sts.windows.net/<tenant-id>/`. 7. Click `Save`, then click `Download VPN client` and deploy the Azure VPN Client profile to every point-to-site user. 8. After every user connects with Microsoft Entra ID, clear `Azure certificate` and `RADIUS authentication`, set `Tunnel type` to `OpenVPN (SSL)`, and click `Save`. 9. Repeat steps 1-8 for each VPN gateway requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each VPN gateway requiring remediation, add Microsoft Entra ID alongside the existing authentication type and protocols:  ``` az network vnet-gateway update --resource-group <resource-group> --name <gateway-name> --client-protocol <existing-protocols> OpenVPN --vpn-auth-type <existing-auth-type> AAD --aad-tenant "https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>" --aad-audience "c632b3df-fb67-4d84-bdcf-b95ad541b5c8" --aad-issuer "https://sts.windows.net/<tenant-id>/" ```  Deploy the Azure VPN Client profile to every user. After all users connect with Microsoft Entra ID, remove the other authentication types:  ``` az network vnet-gateway update --resource-group <resource-group> --name <gateway-name> --client-protocol OpenVPN --vpn-auth-type AAD ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Note:** Some Azure portal builds still label the `Microsoft Entra ID` option `Azure Active Directory`; the API value is `AAD` in both cases.  **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Virtual network gateways`. 2. Click the name of a VPN gateway. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Point-to-site configuration`. 4. Verify that `Authentication type` is set to `Microsoft Entra ID` only, with `Azure certificate` and `RADIUS authentication` not selected. 5. Repeat steps 1-4 for each VPN gateway with a point-to-site configuration.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command for each VPN gateway with a point-to-site configuration:  ``` az network vnet-gateway show --resource-group <resource-group> --name <gateway-name> --query "vpnClientConfiguration.vpnAuthenticationTypes" ```  Verify that the output is `["AAD"]`. An output that includes `Certificate` or `Radius` is non-compliant.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [21a6bc25-125e-4d13-b82d-2e19b7208ab7](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2F21a6bc25-125e-4d13-b82d-2e19b7208ab7) **- Name:** 'VPN gateways should use only Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) authentication for point-to-site users'
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, no authentication type is set; it is chosen when point-to-site is configured.

Requirements.Description: Ensure that Network Security Groups override the default 'VirtualNetwork' allow rules

Attributes.Description: A network security group filters traffic by security rules evaluated in priority order until the first match. By default, the `AllowVnetInBound` and `AllowVnetOutBound` rules permit all traffic identified with the `VirtualNetwork` service tag. A default-deny posture adds an explicit rule, evaluated after every allow rule, that denies all other traffic.  **Prerequisites:** Identify every required inbound and outbound path, including Azure platform traffic such as load balancer health probes, and create narrowly scoped higher-priority allow rules before adding the deny rule.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: The `VirtualNetwork` service tag spans more than the local subnet: Microsoft includes peered virtual networks, on-premises ranges reached over VPN or ExpressRoute, and gateway-connected networks. The default rules also permit unrestricted outbound access to the internet. Relying on them grants lateral reachability across that trust boundary and an open egress path a compromised workload can use for exfiltration or command-and-control.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: An explicit deny-all rule overrides the default `VirtualNetwork` and Internet allow rules, so any inbound or outbound path not covered by a higher-priority allow rule stops working. Required platform traffic must be allowed first, including Azure load balancer health probes inbound and the outbound dependencies of subnet-injected services. Maintaining these allow rules is an ongoing task as connectivity changes.  **Warning:** Do not create an outbound deny-all rule where Microsoft prohibits or advises against outbound restriction, including Application Gateway v2 subnets without Network Isolation and Microsoft Entra Domain Services subnets.  **Note:** Applying the deny rule before the allow rules are in place can sever existing connectivity.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: Complete the prerequisites in the Description before remediating.  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Network security groups`. 2. Click the name of a network security group associated with a workload subnet or network interface. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Inbound security rules`, then click `Add`. 4. Set `Source` to `Any`, `Source port ranges` to `*`, `Destination` to `Any`, `Service` to `Custom`, `Destination port ranges` to `*`, `Protocol` to `Any`, `Action` to `Deny`, and `Priority` to an unused number higher than every existing `Allow` rule, such as the highest free number at or below `4096`. 5. Click `Add`. 6. Under `Settings`, click `Outbound security rules` and repeat steps 3-5 to add an equivalent outbound deny-all rule, unless the subnet is one where Microsoft prohibits or advises against outbound restriction (Application Gateway v2 without Network Isolation, or Microsoft Entra Domain Services). 7. Repeat for each network security group requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  Add the inbound deny-all rule on each in-scope group, and the outbound deny-all rule except where Microsoft prohibits or advises against outbound restriction; use an unused priority higher than the group's allow rules (the highest free number at or below 4096):  ``` az network nsg rule create --resource-group <resource-group> --nsg-name <network-security-group> --name DenyAllInbound --priority <priority> --direction Inbound --access Deny --protocol '*' --source-address-prefixes '*' --source-port-ranges '*' --destination-address-prefixes '*' --destination-port-ranges '*' ```  ``` az network nsg rule create --resource-group <resource-group> --nsg-name <network-security-group> --name DenyAllOutbound --priority <priority> --direction Outbound --access Deny --protocol '*' --source-address-prefixes '*' --source-port-ranges '*' --destination-address-prefixes '*' --destination-port-ranges '*' ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  Add the deny-all rules with an unused priority higher than the group's allow rules, then save the network security group (omit the outbound rule where Microsoft prohibits or advises against outbound restriction):  ``` $nsg = Get-AzNetworkSecurityGroup -Name <network-security-group> -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> Add-AzNetworkSecurityRuleConfig -NetworkSecurityGroup $nsg -Name 'DenyAllInbound' -Access Deny -Protocol '*' -Direction Inbound -Priority <priority> -SourceAddressPrefix '*' -SourcePortRange '*' -DestinationAddressPrefix '*' -DestinationPortRange '*' Add-AzNetworkSecurityRuleConfig -NetworkSecurityGroup $nsg -Name 'DenyAllOutbound' -Access Deny -Protocol '*' -Direction Outbound -Priority <priority> -SourceAddressPrefix '*' -SourcePortRange '*' -DestinationAddressPrefix '*' -DestinationPortRange '*' Set-AzNetworkSecurityGroup -NetworkSecurityGroup $nsg ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Network security groups`. 2. Click the name of a network security group associated with a workload subnet or network interface. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Inbound security rules`. 4. Confirm a user-defined rule exists with `Source` set to `Any`, `Source port ranges` set to `*`, `Destination` set to `Any`, `Service` set to `Custom` with `Destination port ranges` of `*`, `Protocol` set to `Any`, and `Action` set to `Deny`, at a priority number higher than (evaluated after) every user-defined `Allow` rule. 5. Under `Settings`, click `Outbound security rules` and confirm an equivalent deny-all rule exists, except where Microsoft prohibits or advises against outbound restriction (Application Gateway v2 without Network Isolation, and Microsoft Entra Domain Services). 6. Repeat for each network security group, excluding platform-managed subnets such as `GatewaySubnet` (which must not have a network security group), `AzureBastionSubnet`, `AzureFirewallSubnet`, and `RouteServerSubnet`.  To screen the whole estate from Azure Resource Graph, run the following query and review each returned network security group against the scope exclusions above:  ``` resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/networksecuritygroups' | mv-expand rule = iff(array_length(properties.securityRules) > 0, properties.securityRules, dynamic([null])) limit 1000 | extend r = rule.properties | extend access = tostring(r.access), direction = tostring(r.direction), priority = toint(r.priority), srcAny = (tostring(r.sourceAddressPrefix) == '*' or array_index_of(r.sourceAddressPrefixes, '*') >= 0), dstAny = (tostring(r.destinationAddressPrefix) == '*' or array_index_of(r.destinationAddressPrefixes, '*') >= 0), sportAny = (tostring(r.sourcePortRange) == '*' or array_index_of(r.sourcePortRanges, '*') >= 0), dportAny = (tostring(r.destinationPortRange) == '*' or array_index_of(r.destinationPortRanges, '*') >= 0), protoAny = (tostring(r.protocol) == '*') | extend isDenyAll = (access =~ 'Deny' and srcAny and dstAny and sportAny and dportAny and protoAny), isAllow = (access =~ 'Allow') | summarize inDeny = maxif(priority, isDenyAll and direction =~ 'Inbound'), outDeny = maxif(priority, isDenyAll and direction =~ 'Outbound'), inAllow = maxif(priority, isAllow and direction =~ 'Inbound'), outAllow = maxif(priority, isAllow and direction =~ 'Outbound') by id, name | where isnull(inDeny) or isnull(outDeny) or inDeny <= coalesce(inAllow, -1) or outDeny <= coalesce(outAllow, -1) ```  A returned network security group is missing an inbound or outbound deny-all rule, or has one that is not evaluated after every `Allow` rule.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  List the deny-all rules on each network security group:  ``` az network nsg rule list --resource-group <resource-group> --nsg-name <network-security-group> --query "[?access=='Deny' && protocol=='*' && (sourceAddressPrefix=='*' || contains(sourceAddressPrefixes || \`[]\`, '*')) && (sourcePortRange=='*' || contains(sourcePortRanges || \`[]\`, '*')) && (destinationAddressPrefix=='*' || contains(destinationAddressPrefixes || \`[]\`, '*')) && (destinationPortRange=='*' || contains(destinationPortRanges || \`[]\`, '*'))].{Name:name, Direction:direction, Priority:priority}" --output table ```  List the highest `Allow` priority per direction:  ``` az network nsg rule list --resource-group <resource-group> --nsg-name <network-security-group> --query "[?access=='Allow'].{Direction:direction, Priority:priority}" --output table ```  Ensure a deny-all rule is returned for both `Inbound` and `Outbound`, each at a priority higher than the highest `Allow` priority in the same direction.  **Audit from PowerShell**  List the deny-all rules on each network security group:  ``` $nsg = Get-AzNetworkSecurityGroup -Name <network-security-group> -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> $nsg.SecurityRules | Where-Object { $_.Access -eq 'Deny' -and $_.Protocol -eq '*' -and $_.SourceAddressPrefix -contains '*' -and $_.SourcePortRange -contains '*' -and $_.DestinationAddressPrefix -contains '*' -and $_.DestinationPortRange -contains '*' } | Select-Object Name, Direction, Priority ```  List the highest `Allow` priority per direction:  ``` $nsg.SecurityRules | Where-Object { $_.Access -eq 'Allow' } | Group-Object Direction | ForEach-Object { [pscustomobject]@{ Direction = $_.Name; MaxAllowPriority = ($_.Group.Priority | Measure-Object -Maximum).Maximum } } ```  Ensure a deny-all rule is listed for both `Inbound` and `Outbound`, each at a priority higher than the highest `Allow` priority in the same direction.
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: User-defined rule priorities range from 100 to 4096, while the default rules occupy 65000 to 65500, so any user rule overrides the default allows. Augmented security rules, available only in the Resource Manager model, let a single rule carry multiple IP ranges and ports, reducing the number of allow rules needed. When a network security group is applied to both a subnet and a network interface, traffic must be permitted by both for it to pass.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, a network security group has no user rules; its default rules allow `VirtualNetwork`, inbound load balancer, and outbound Internet traffic, and deny all else.

Requirements.Description: Ensure Azure Network Security Perimeter is Used to Secure Azure Platform-as-a-service Resources

Attributes.Description: A network security perimeter association places a PaaS resource in one of three access modes: `Transition` (API value `Learning`), which falls back to the resource's firewall when no perimeter rule matches; `Audit`, which logs access decisions; or `Enforced`, which applies only perimeter rules. The `Access mode` setting selects among them.  **Note:** Although this recommendation can be audited by command, it is Manual because which resources belong in which perimeter and profile depends on each organization.  **Prerequisites:** Enable the perimeter's diagnostic logs, review them in `Transition` mode, and add access rules for every legitimate caller before setting `Enforced`, or that traffic is denied.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: In `Transition` mode, an associated resource stays reachable through any public access its own firewall allows, and its outbound calls are not limited to perimeter rules. An attacker holding a valid credential can therefore read or move data over the public endpoint while the association suggests a boundary that is not enforced.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: In `Enforced` mode, the perimeter denies any request no access rule allows: trusted Azure service exceptions are not honored, intra-perimeter calls need a managed identity on the caller, and basic service endpoint traffic can be denied even when an inbound rule allows every address. Virtual network workloads therefore need private endpoints or, where supported, standard service endpoints.  **Warning:** Associating a resource in any access mode breaks Azure Backup for storage accounts and disables analytic rules on Log Analytics workspaces enabled for Microsoft Sentinel, so those resources are excluded from this recommendation.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: Complete the prerequisites in the Description before remediating.  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  Create and associate PaaS resources with a new network security perimeter:  1. Go to `Network Security Perimeters`. 2. Click `+ Create`. 3. Select a `Subscription` and `Resource group`, provide a `Name`, select a `Region`, and provide a `Profile name`. 4. Click `Next`. 5. Click `+ Add`. 6. Check the box next to a PaaS resource to associate it with the network security perimeter. 7. Click `Select`. 8. Click `Next`. 9. Configure appropriate `Inbound access rules` for your organization. 10. Click `Next`. 11. Configure appropriate `Outbound access rules` for your organization. 12. Click `Review + create`. 13. Click `Create`.  Associate PaaS resources with an existing network security perimeter:  1. Go to `Network Security Perimeters`. 2. Click the name of a network security perimeter. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Associated resources`. 4. Click `+ Add`. 5. Select `Associate resources with a new profile` or `Associate resources with an existing profile`. 6. To associate resources with a new profile: a) Provide a `Name`. b) Click `Next`. c) Click `+ Add`. d) Check the box next to a PaaS resource to associate it with the network security perimeter. e) Click `Select`. f) Click `Next`. g) Configure appropriate `Inbound access rules` for your organization. h) Click `Next`. i) Configure appropriate `Outbound access rules` for your organization. j) Click `Review + create`. k) Click `Create`. 7. To associate resources with an existing profile: a) Next to `Profile`, click `Select` to display the drop-down menu. b) Select a profile. c) Click `+ Add`. d) Check the box next to a PaaS resource to associate it with the network security perimeter. e) Click `Select`. f) Click `Associate`.  Enforce each association and remove unrestricted inbound rules:  1. Go to `Network Security Perimeters`. 2. Click the name of a network security perimeter. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Associated resources`. 4. Click the `...` at the end of an associated resource's row, then click `Change access mode`. 5. Select `Enforced`, then click `Apply`. 6. Repeat steps 4-5 for each associated resource. 7. Under `Settings`, click `Profiles`, click each profile, and remove any inbound access rule that allows `0.0.0.0/0`.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  1. If no suitable network security perimeter exists, run the following command to create one:  ``` az network perimeter create --resource-group <resource-group> --name <network-security-perimeter> --location <location> ```  2. Run the following command to list the perimeter's profiles:  ``` az network perimeter profile list --resource-group <resource-group> --perimeter-name <network-security-perimeter> ```  3. If no suitable profile exists, run the following command to create one:  ``` az network perimeter profile create --resource-group <resource-group> --perimeter-name <network-security-perimeter> --name <profile> ```  4. For each legitimate inbound caller, run the following command to create an access rule:  ``` az network perimeter profile access-rule create --resource-group <resource-group> --perimeter-name <network-security-perimeter> --profile-name <profile> --access-rule-name <access-rule> --direction Inbound --address-prefixes "<address-prefix>" ```  5. For each noted resource without an association, run the following command to associate it in `Enforced` mode:  ``` az network perimeter association create --resource-group <resource-group> --perimeter-name <network-security-perimeter> --association-name <association> --private-link-resource "{id:<paas-resource-id>}" --profile "{id:<profile-id>}" --access-mode Enforced ```  6. For each existing association not in `Enforced` mode, run the following command:  ``` az network perimeter association update --resource-group <resource-group> --perimeter-name <network-security-perimeter> --association-name <association> --access-mode Enforced ```  7. For each inbound access rule that allows `0.0.0.0/0`, run the following command to delete it:  ``` az network perimeter profile access-rule delete --resource-group <resource-group> --perimeter-name <network-security-perimeter> --profile-name <profile> --access-rule-name <access-rule> ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Resource groups`. 2. Click the name of a resource group. 3. Take note of resources of the generally available types listed in Additional Information, excluding storage accounts protected by Azure Backup and Log Analytics workspaces enabled for Microsoft Sentinel. 4. Repeat steps 1-3 for each resource group in each subscription in scope. 5. Go to `Network Security Perimeters`. 6. Click the name of a network security perimeter. 7. Under `Settings`, click `Associated resources`, and take note of each associated resource and its access mode. 8. Under `Settings`, click `Profiles`, click each profile, and take note of its `Inbound access rules`. 9. Repeat steps 6-8 for each network security perimeter in each subscription in scope. 10. Verify each noted resource is associated with a network security perimeter with an access mode of `Enforced`, and that no inbound access rule allows `0.0.0.0/0`.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  1. Run the following command to list resource groups:  ``` az group list --query "[].name" ```  2. For each resource group, run the following command to list its resources, and take note of resources of the generally available types listed in Additional Information, excluding storage accounts protected by Azure Backup and Log Analytics workspaces enabled for Microsoft Sentinel:  ``` az resource list --resource-group <resource-group> --query "[].{name:name, type:type, id:id}" ```  3. For each resource group, run the following command to list network security perimeters:  ``` az network perimeter list --resource-group <resource-group> ```  4. For each network security perimeter, run the following command to list its associations:  ``` az network perimeter association list --resource-group <resource-group> --perimeter-name <network-security-perimeter> ```  5. For each profile of each network security perimeter, run the following command to list its access rules:  ``` az network perimeter profile access-rule list --resource-group <resource-group> --perimeter-name <network-security-perimeter> --profile-name <profile> ```  6. Repeat steps 1-5 for each subscription in scope; a perimeter may reside in a different resource group or subscription than the resources it secures. 7. Verify each noted resource ID appears as the `privateLinkResource.id` of an association whose `accessMode` is `Enforced`, and that no inbound access rule's `addressPrefixes` include `0.0.0.0/0`. Any other `accessMode` value, including `Learning` or `Audit`, is non-compliant.
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: Resources that can be associated are Azure Monitor, Azure AI Search, Event Hubs, Key Vault, Storage, Microsoft Foundry, and Service Bus; App Configuration, Cosmos DB, SQL Database, Azure OpenAI Service, and Event Grid are in public preview and outside this recommendation. Private endpoint traffic needs no access rule. SAS tokens are rejected for intra-perimeter traffic and subscription-based inbound rules. A paid standard service endpoint can admit virtual network workloads to Storage, Key Vault, SQL Database, and Cosmos DB through an IP-based inbound rule on its public IP network identifier.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, PaaS resources are not associated with a network security perimeter, and a new association's access mode is `Transition`.

Requirements.Description: Ensure Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) is Enabled on Azure Front Door

Attributes.Description: Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) on Azure Front Door inspects incoming HTTP and HTTPS requests at the Microsoft network edge and blocks common exploits before they reach the origin. Ensure every domain served by an Azure Front Door Standard or Premium profile is associated with an enabled WAF policy.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Applications published through Azure Front Door are reachable from the internet, so injection, cross-site scripting, malicious bot, and HTTP flood traffic arrives at the edge first. A WAF policy blocks these requests before they reach the origin, and Microsoft updates its managed rule sets as new attack signatures appear.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: A WAF policy in Prevention mode can block legitimate requests, so run a new policy in Detection mode and tune it before switching to Prevention. Azure-managed rule sets and bot protection require the Premium tier; the Standard tier supports custom rules only. WAF policies and inspected requests add cost, and rule tuning adds operational effort.  **Warning:** Azure Front Door (classic) retires on 31 March 2027; migrate classic profiles to Standard or Premium.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Click `Create a resource`, search for `Web Application Firewall (WAF)`, select it, and click `Create`. 2. On the `Basics` tab, set `Policy for` to `Global WAF (Front Door)`, set `Front door tier` to the tier of the profile, and set `Policy state` to `Enabled`. 3. On the `Managed rules` and `Policy settings` tabs, configure the rule sets and settings the application requires. 4. On the `Association` tab, click `Associate a Front door profile`, select the profile, set `Association scope` to `Domain`, select every domain in the profile, and click `Add`. 5. Click `Review + create`, then click `Create`. 6. Repeat steps 1-5 for each Azure Front Door profile requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to create a WAF policy. For a Standard tier profile, use `Standard_AzureFrontDoor` as the SKU:  ``` az network front-door waf-policy create --name <waf-policy-name> --resource-group <resource-group> --sku Premium_AzureFrontDoor --disabled false --mode Prevention ```  Run the following command to associate the WAF policy with the profile's domains, listing every endpoint and custom domain ID:  ``` az afd security-policy create --resource-group <resource-group> --profile-name <profile-name> --security-policy-name <security-policy-name> --domains <domain-id-1> <domain-id-2> --waf-policy <waf-policy-id> ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Front Door and CDN profiles`. 2. Click the name of an Azure Front Door Standard or Premium profile. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Front Door manager`. 4. For each endpoint, ensure every domain listed, including the endpoint's default domain, is covered by a security policy that references a WAF policy. 5. Click each referenced WAF policy and ensure its policy state is `Enabled`. 6. Repeat steps 1-5 for each Azure Front Door profile.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list Azure Front Door profiles:  ``` az afd profile list --query "[].{name:name, resourceGroup:resourceGroup, sku:sku.name}" --output table ```  For each profile, run the following commands to list the endpoint and custom domain IDs:  ``` az afd endpoint list --resource-group <resource-group> --profile-name <profile-name> --query "[].id" --output tsv ```  ``` az afd custom-domain list --resource-group <resource-group> --profile-name <profile-name> --query "[].id" --output tsv ```  Run the following command to list the profile's security policies:  ``` az afd security-policy list --resource-group <resource-group> --profile-name <profile-name> ```  Ensure every endpoint and custom domain ID returned above appears in the domain associations of a security policy that references a WAF policy ID. For each referenced WAF policy, run the following command:  ``` az network front-door waf-policy show --ids <waf-policy-id> --query "policySettings.enabledState" ```  Ensure `Enabled` is returned.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [055aa869-bc98-4af8-bafc-23f1ab6ffe2c](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2F055aa869-bc98-4af8-bafc-23f1ab6ffe2c) **- Name:** 'Azure Web Application Firewall should be enabled for Azure Front Door entry-points'  **Note:** This Policy evaluates only Azure Front Door (classic) profiles, not Standard or Premium profiles, so use the Azure Portal or Azure CLI method for those.
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: A custom rule with the `Allow` action stops evaluation of the Default Rule Set and the Bot Protection rule set for matching requests, so scope Allow rules as narrowly as possible.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, no WAF policy is associated with an Azure Front Door profile.

Requirements.Description: Ensure 'Default outbound access' is Set to 'Disabled' for Virtual Network Subnets

Attributes.Description: Virtual machines without an explicit outbound method reach public endpoints through default outbound access, a Microsoft-owned public IP address, unless their subnet is private. The subnet's `Default outbound access` setting is `Enabled` or `Disabled` (private); delegated subnets and the subnets reserved for gateways, Azure Firewall, Route Server, and Bastion are out of scope.  **Prerequisites:** Give each virtual machine that needs public endpoints an explicit outbound method, such as a NAT gateway, before disabling default outbound access.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Default outbound access gives a virtual machine an internet egress path nobody configured, through a Microsoft-owned public IP address that can change without notice. A compromised workload can use that path for data exfiltration or command-and-control traffic that leaves from an address the organization does not own and passes through no egress firewall or NAT gateway it controls.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Virtual machines without an explicit outbound method lose access to the internet and to public Microsoft endpoints, including Windows activation and Windows Update, once they are stopped and deallocated after the change. User-defined routes with next hop type `Internet` stop working in a private subnet. An explicit outbound method such as a NAT gateway adds cost and management effort.  **Warning:** Microsoft is retiring default outbound access as the default: in API versions released after March 31, 2026, subnets in new virtual networks are private unless set otherwise, and existing virtual networks keep their current setting.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: Complete the prerequisites in the Description before remediating.  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Virtual networks`. 2. Click the name of a virtual network. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Subnets`. 4. Click the name of a subnet requiring remediation. 5. Set `Default outbound access` to `Disabled`. 6. Click `Save`. 7. Repeat steps 1-6 for each virtual network and subnet requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each subnet requiring remediation, run the following command to make it private:  ``` az network vnet subnet update --resource-group <resource-group> --vnet-name <virtual-network> --name <subnet> --default-outbound false ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each subnet requiring remediation, run the following commands to make it private:  ``` $vnet = Get-AzVirtualNetwork -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <virtual-network> ($vnet.Subnets | Where-Object { $_.Name -eq '<subnet>' }).DefaultOutboundAccess = $false $vnet | Set-AzVirtualNetwork ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Virtual networks`. 2. Click the name of a virtual network. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Subnets`. 4. Click the name of a subnet that is not delegated to a service and is not `GatewaySubnet`, `AzureFirewallSubnet`, `AzureFirewallManagementSubnet`, `RouteServerSubnet`, or `AzureBastionSubnet`. 5. Ensure `Default outbound access` is set to `Disabled`. 6.
