Requirements.Description: Ensure that Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Monitoring (EASM) is Enabled

Attributes.Description: An organization's attack surface is the collection of assets with a public network identifier or URI that an external threat actor can see or access from outside your cloud. It is the set of points on the boundary of a system, a system element, system component, or an environment where an attacker can try to enter, cause an effect on, or extract data from, that system, system element, system component, or environment. The larger the attack surface, the harder it is to protect.  This tool can be configured to scan your organization's online infrastructure such as specified domains, hosts, CIDR blocks, and SSL certificates, and store them in an Inventory. Inventory items can be added, reviewed, approved, and removed, and may contain enrichments ("insights") and additional information collected from the tool's different scan engines and open-source intelligence sources.  A Defender EASM workspace will generate an Inventory of publicly exposed assets by crawling and scanning the internet using Seeds you provide when setting up the tool. Seeds can be FQDNs, IP CIDR blocks, and WHOIS records.  Defender EASM will generate Insights within 24-48 hours after Seeds are provided, and these insights include vulnerability data (CVEs), ports and protocols, and weak or expired SSL certificates that could be used by an attacker for reconnaissance or exploitation.  Results are classified High/Medium/Low and some of them include proposed mitigations.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: This tool can monitor the externally exposed resources of an organization, provide valuable insights, and export these findings in a variety of formats (including CSV) for use in vulnerability management operations and red/purple team exercises.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Microsoft Defender EASM workspaces are currently available as Azure Resources with a 30-day free trial period but can quickly accrue significant charges. The costs are calculated daily as (Number of "billable" inventory items) x (item cost per day).  Estimated cost is not provided within the tool, and users are strongly advised to contact their Microsoft sales representative for pricing and set a calendar reminder for the end of the trial period.  If the workspace is deleted by the last day of a free trial period, no charges are billed.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Microsoft Defender EASM`. 2. Click `+ Create`. 3. Under `Project details`, select a subscription. 4. Select or create a resource group. 5. Under `Instance details`, enter a name for the workspace. 6. Select a region. 7. Click `Review + create`. 8. Click `Create`. 9. Once the deployment has completed, go to `Microsoft Defender EASM`. 10. Click the workspace name. 11. Configure the workspace appropriately for your environment and organization.
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Microsoft Defender EASM`. 2. Ensure that at least one Microsoft Defender EASM workspace is listed. 3. Click the name of a workspace. 4. Ensure the workspace is configured appropriately for your environment and organization. 5. Repeat steps 3-4 for each workspace.
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: Microsoft added its Defender for External Attack Surface management (EASM) offering to Azure following its 2022 acquisition of EASM SaaS tool company RiskIQ.
Attributes.DefaultValue: Microsoft Defender EASM is an optional, paid Azure Resource that must be created and configured inside a Subscription and Resource Group.

Requirements.Description: Ensure That Microsoft Defender for IoT Hub Is Set To 'On'

Attributes.Description: Microsoft Defender for IoT acts as a central security hub for IoT devices within your organization.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: IoT devices are very rarely patched and can be potential attack vectors for enterprise networks. Updating their network configuration to use a central security hub allows for detection of these breaches.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Enabling Microsoft Defender for IoT will incur additional charges dependent on the level of usage.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `IoT Hub`. 2. Select an `IoT Hub` to validate. 3. Select `Overview` in `Defender for IoT`. 4. Click on `Secure your IoT solution`, and complete the onboarding.
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `IoT Hub`. 2. Select an `IoT Hub` to validate. 3. Select `Overview` in `Defender for IoT`. 4. The Threat prevention and Threat detection screen will appear, if `Defender for IoT` is Enabled.
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: There are additional configurations for Microsoft Defender for IoT that allow for types of deployments called hybrid or local. Both run on your physical infrastructure. These are complicated setups and are primarily outside of the scope of a purely Azure benchmark. Please see the references to consider these options for your organization.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, Microsoft Defender for IoT is not enabled.

Requirements.Description: Ensure that Azure Key Vault Managed HSM is Used when Required

Attributes.Description: Key Vault Premium uses multitenant HSMs that Microsoft operates; Managed HSM is a single-tenant HSM pool with a customer-owned security domain. Managed HSM and Premium key versions on HSM Platform 2 are FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated; Premium key versions on HSM Platform 1 are FIPS 140-2 Level 2.  **Note:** Although this recommendation can be audited by command, it is Manual because it applies only where a regulatory or contractual requirement mandates a dedicated, customer-controlled HSM.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: On Key Vault Premium, the HSMs and the root of trust are shared and operated by Microsoft, and cryptographic operations are throttled at multitenant limits. Where a requirement mandates key sovereignty, single tenancy, or a customer-owned root of trust, keys held in Premium do not meet it, whatever their FIPS validation level.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Managed HSM is billed hourly per HSM pool plus monthly per HSM-protected key version; see https://azure.microsoft.com/pricing/details/key-vault/. Billing continues through the soft-delete retention period until the HSM is purged. The customer holds the security domain: without it and its quorum of wrapping keys, every key in the HSM is unrecoverable after a disaster or a purge.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Requisite Permissions - read section overview!**  Creating a Managed HSM needs Azure Resource Manager permissions. Downloading the security domain to activate it needs the Managed HSM local RBAC role `Managed HSM Administrator`, which the administrators named at creation hold.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to store the object ID of the signed-in user, or prepare a space-separated list of administrator object IDs instead:  ``` oid=$(az ad signed-in-user show --query id --output tsv) ```  Run the following command to create a Managed HSM:  ``` az keyvault create --resource-group <resource-group> --hsm-name <hsm-name> --location <location> --retention-days <retention-days> --administrators $oid ```  The HSM must then be activated by downloading its security domain, encrypted with at least three and at most ten RSA public keys. Generate each key pair, for example with OpenSSL:  ``` openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout cert_1.key -x509 -days 365 -out cert_1.cer ```  As an HSM administrator, run the following command to download the security domain and activate the Managed HSM, setting `--sd-quorum` to the number of private keys required to decrypt it:  ``` az keyvault security-domain download --hsm-name <hsm-name> --sd-wrapping-keys <cert-1>.cer <cert-2>.cer <cert-3>.cer --sd-quorum <quorum> --security-domain-file <hsm-name>-SD.json ```  Store the security domain file and the RSA private keys offline under separate custody; they are required for disaster recovery.
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Requisite Permissions - read section overview!**  Listing Managed HSMs needs only Azure Resource Manager read access. Listing the keys in a Managed HSM needs the Managed HSM local RBAC role `Managed HSM Crypto Auditor`.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list Managed HSMs:  ``` az keyvault list --resource-type hsm --query "[].{name:name, resourceGroup:resourceGroup, location:location}" ```  For each Managed HSM, run the following command to list its keys:  ``` az keyvault key list --hsm-name <hsm-name> ```  Where a requirement mandates a dedicated HSM, verify that at least one Managed HSM is returned and that the keys in scope of the requirement are listed in it.
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: Two Managed HSM capabilities address specific key custody requirements. External key management keeps key-encryption keys in a customer-operated HSM outside Microsoft infrastructure, reached through a customer-run proxy. Microsoft positions it as a last resort for a legal or contractual custody requirement: the proxy and external HSM fall outside the Managed HSM service-level agreement, and external keys support no geo-replication, backup and restore, or Secure Key Release. Keyless TLS lets Application Gateway v2 terminate TLS with a certificate whose private key stays in Managed HSM.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, no Managed HSM exists in a subscription.

Requirements.Description: Ensure that Logging for Azure Key Vault Managed HSM is 'Enabled'

Attributes.Description: A Managed HSM keeps its `AuditEvent` resource log, the record of authenticated requests and key operations, only when a diagnostic setting sends that log category to a Log Analytics workspace, storage account, or event hub.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Without a diagnostic setting, the HSM's key operations, local role assignment changes, and security domain downloads leave no retained record. Misuse of a key, an over-broad role assignment, or a security domain export by an insider then cannot be detected or attributed, for the keys that protect an estate's most sensitive data.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: The destination bills for the exported logs: ingestion and retention charges apply in a Log Analytics workspace, and storage or throughput charges apply to a storage account or event hub.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Managed HSM Pools`. 2. Click the name of a Managed HSM. 3. Under `Monitoring`, click `Diagnostic settings`. 4. Click `Edit setting` next to a diagnostic setting, or click `Add diagnostic setting` and enter a `Diagnostic setting name`. 5. Under `Category groups`, check `audit`. 6. Under `Destination details`, select at least one destination. 7. Click `Save`. 8. Repeat steps 1-7 for each Managed HSM requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each Managed HSM requiring remediation, run the following command:  ``` az monitor diagnostic-settings create --name <diagnostic-setting-name> --resource <managed-hsm-resource-id> --workspace <log-analytics-workspace-resource-id> --logs '[{"category":"AuditEvent","enabled":true}]' ```  - To update an existing setting, use its name and supply all of its existing destinations, log categories, and metrics (`--metrics`) again, because the command replaces the whole setting. - For a storage account or event hub destination, replace `--workspace` with `--storage-account <storage-account-resource-id>` or `--event-hub <event-hub-name> --event-hub-rule <event-hub-authorization-rule-id>`.  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each Managed HSM requiring remediation, run the following commands:  ``` $logSettings = New-AzDiagnosticSettingLogSettingsObject -Enabled $true -Category AuditEvent New-AzDiagnosticSetting -Name <diagnostic-setting-name> -ResourceId <managed-hsm-resource-id> -WorkspaceId <log-analytics-workspace-resource-id> -Log $logSettings ```  - To update an existing setting, use its name and supply all of its existing destinations, log categories, and metrics (`-Metric`) again, because the command replaces the whole setting. - For a storage account or event hub destination, replace `-WorkspaceId` with `-StorageAccountId <storage-account-resource-id>` or `-EventHubName <event-hub-name> -EventHubAuthorizationRuleId <event-hub-authorization-rule-id>`.
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Note:** Data-plane access is not required; Azure Resource Manager read access is sufficient.  **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Managed HSM Pools`. 2. Click the name of a Managed HSM. 3. Under `Monitoring`, click `Diagnostic settings`. 4. Click `Edit setting` next to a diagnostic setting. 5. Ensure that a destination is configured. 6. Ensure that `audit` or `allLogs` is checked under `Category groups`, or that the `AuditEvent` category is checked. 7. Repeat steps 1-6 for each Managed HSM.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  List Managed HSMs:  ``` az keyvault list --resource-type hsm --query "[].id" --output tsv ```  For each Managed HSM, list its diagnostic settings:  ``` az monitor diagnostic-settings list --resource <managed-hsm-resource-id> ```  Ensure that at least one setting has a destination (`workspaceId`, `storageAccountId`, `eventHubAuthorizationRuleId`, or `marketplacePartnerId`) and an enabled `logs` entry for the `audit` or `allLogs` category group or the `AuditEvent` category.  **Audit from PowerShell**  List Managed HSMs:  ``` Get-AzKeyVaultManagedHsm | Select-Object Name, ResourceId ```  For each Managed HSM, list its diagnostic settings:  ``` Get-AzDiagnosticSetting -ResourceId <managed-hsm-resource-id> | Select-Object Name, WorkspaceId, StorageAccountId, EventHubAuthorizationRuleId, MarketplacePartnerId, @{Name = 'EnabledLogs'; Expression = { ($_.Log | Where-Object { $_.Enabled } | ForEach-Object { if ($_.CategoryGroup) { $_.CategoryGroup } else { $_.Category } }) -join ', ' }} ```  Ensure that at least one setting shows a destination and `EnabledLogs` containing `audit`, `allLogs`, or `AuditEvent`.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [a2a5b911-5617-447e-a49e-59dbe0e0434b](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2Fa2a5b911-5617-447e-a49e-59dbe0e0434b) **- Name:** 'Resource logs in Azure Key Vault Managed HSM should be enabled'  This Policy does not check the destination, and it reports a setting that sends logs to a storage account with legacy retention enabled for fewer than 365 days as non-compliant; confirm those cases with the Azure CLI or PowerShell method.
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: The recommendation 'Ensure that Logging for Azure Key Vault is 'Enabled'' covers key vaults; neither it nor its cited Azure Policy evaluates Managed HSM, a separate resource type. `AuditEvent` is the only Managed HSM log category, so the `audit` and `allLogs` category groups collect the same records.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, a Managed HSM has no diagnostic setting, so its `AuditEvent` log is not kept.

Requirements.Description: Ensure Keys in Azure Key Vault Premium are HSM-Protected

Attributes.Description: A key in a Premium-tier key vault is software-protected, with key type `RSA` or `EC`, or HSM-protected, with key type `RSA-HSM`, `EC-HSM`, or `oct-HSM`. The key type chosen when each key is created selects between them. Keys that back certificates follow the certificate's key type and are out of scope.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Key Vault Premium accepts software-protected keys beside HSM-protected ones, and a software-protected key carries FIPS 140-2 Level 1 validation rather than the FIPS 140-3 Level 3 of HSM-protected key versions on HSM Platform 2. A vault chosen for HSM protection can therefore hold keys protected only to FIPS 140-2 Level 1, short of what a hardware key protection requirement demands.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: HSM-protected keys are billed per key each month in addition to per-operation charges; see the Key Vault pricing page. Remediation creates a new HSM-protected key, and every service or application that uses the software-protected key must be moved to it before the old key is disabled.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Note:** Creating and disabling keys needs the `Key Vault Crypto Officer` role, or the `Create` and `Update` key permissions on a vault that uses access policies.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each software-protected `RSA` key, create an HSM-protected replacement of the same size (for an `EC` key, use `--kty EC-HSM --curve <curve>`):  ``` az keyvault key create --vault-name <key-vault> --name <new-key-name> --kty RSA-HSM --size <key-size> ```  Move each workload that uses the software-protected key to the new key, then disable the software-protected key:  ``` az keyvault key set-attributes --vault-name <key-vault> --name <key-name> --enabled false ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each software-protected `RSA` key, create an HSM-protected replacement of the same size (for an `EC` key, use `-KeyType EC -CurveName <curve>`):  ``` Add-AzKeyVaultKey -VaultName <key-vault> -Name <new-key-name> -Destination HSM -KeyType RSA -Size <key-size> ```  Move each workload that uses the software-protected key to the new key, then disable the software-protected key:  ``` Update-AzKeyVaultKey -VaultName <key-vault> -Name <key-name> -Enable $false ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Note:** These procedures read keys through each vault's data plane, which needs the `Key Vault Reader` role (or the `Get` and `List` key permissions on a vault that uses access policies) and a client on a network the vault's firewall allows.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to get a vault's pricing tier:  ``` az keyvault show --resource-group <resource-group> --name <key-vault> --query properties.sku.name --output tsv ```  For a `premium` vault, list its enabled keys (certificate keys are excluded by default):  ``` az keyvault key list --vault-name <key-vault> --query '[?attributes.enabled].name' --output tsv ```  For each key, get its key type:  ``` az keyvault key show --vault-name <key-vault> --name <key-name> --query key.kty --output tsv ```  Ensure that each key returns `RSA-HSM`, `EC-HSM`, or `oct-HSM`.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Run the following command to get a key vault's pricing tier:  ``` (Get-AzKeyVault -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -VaultName <key-vault>).Sku ```  For a `Premium` vault, get the key type of each enabled key that does not share a certificate's name:  ``` $certificates = (Get-AzKeyVaultCertificate -VaultName <key-vault>).Name Get-AzKeyVaultKey -VaultName <key-vault> | Where-Object { $_.Enabled -and $_.Name -notin $certificates } | ForEach-Object { Get-AzKeyVaultKey -VaultName <key-vault> -Name $_.Name } | Select-Object Name, KeyType ```  Ensure that each key reports `RSA-HSM`, `EC-HSM`, or `oct-HSM`.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [587c79fe-dd04-4a5e-9d0b-f89598c7261b](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2F587c79fe-dd04-4a5e-9d0b-f89598c7261b) **- Name:** 'Keys should be backed by a hardware security module (HSM)'
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: The cited Azure Policy evaluates every key in every vault, so it also reports keys in Standard-tier vaults, `oct-HSM` keys (in preview in Key Vault Premium), disabled keys, including keys disabled by this remediation, and possibly keys that back certificates. Assign it at scopes that hold Premium vaults and treat those results as outside this recommendation. A certificate key follows its certificate policy, and an exportable certificate key is software-protected by design.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, a Premium-tier key vault accepts both software-protected and HSM-protected keys.

Requirements.Description: Ensure 'Purge protection' is Set to 'Enabled' for Azure Key Vault Managed HSM

Attributes.Description: A deleted Managed HSM and its deleted keys stay recoverable for a soft-delete retention period of 7 to 90 days. The `Purge protection` setting, `Enabled` or `Disabled`, decides whether a deleted HSM or key can be purged, which deletes it permanently, before that period ends.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: With purge protection disabled, a Managed HSM Contributor can delete and immediately purge the HSM, and a Managed HSM Crypto Officer can do the same to its keys. Unless a full HSM backup and its security domain are held, the key material is destroyed and all data encrypted with it becomes permanently unreadable, whether by mistake or sabotage.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Enabling purge protection cannot be reversed. A deleted HSM can then no longer be purged before its retention period ends, so its name cannot be reused and it keeps accruing hourly charges until it is recovered or the period expires.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Note:** Enabling purge protection requires Azure Resource Manager write access to the Managed HSM, such as the `Managed HSM Contributor` role, and cannot be reversed.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each Managed HSM requiring remediation, run the following command to enable purge protection:  ``` az keyvault update-hsm --resource-group <resource-group> --hsm-name <hsm-name> --enable-purge-protection true ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each Managed HSM requiring remediation, run the following command to enable purge protection:  ``` Update-AzKeyVaultManagedHsm -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <hsm-name> -EnablePurgeProtection ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Note:** Data-plane access is not required; Azure Resource Manager read access is sufficient. No Azure Portal method is given: the portal `Properties` page shows purge protection, but Microsoft documents enabling it for Managed HSM through Azure CLI and PowerShell only.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list Managed HSMs:  ``` az keyvault list --resource-type hsm --query "[].{name:name, resourceGroup:resourceGroup}" --output table ```  For each Managed HSM, run the following command to get the purge protection setting:  ``` az keyvault show --resource-group <resource-group> --hsm-name <hsm-name> --query properties.enablePurgeProtection --output tsv ```  Ensure that `true` is returned.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Run the following command to list Managed HSMs:  ``` Get-AzKeyVaultManagedHsm ```  For each Managed HSM, run the following command to get the purge protection setting:  ``` Get-AzKeyVaultManagedHsm -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <hsm-name> | Select-Object Name, EnablePurgeProtection ```  Ensure that `EnablePurgeProtection` is `True`.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [c39ba22d-4428-4149-b981-70acb31fc383](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2Fc39ba22d-4428-4149-b981-70acb31fc383) **- Name:** 'Azure Key Vault Managed HSM should have purge protection enabled'
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: The recommendation 'Ensure 'Purge protection' is Set to 'Enabled'' covers key vaults; neither it nor its cited Azure Policy evaluates Managed HSM, a separate resource type. Soft delete is always on for Managed HSM and cannot be disabled, and the cited Azure Policy checks it as well. The retention period cannot be changed after the HSM is created.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, purge protection is disabled on a new Managed HSM.

Requirements.Description: Ensure 'Public Network Access' is 'Disabled' for Azure Key Vault Managed HSM

Attributes.Description: A Managed HSM accepts data-plane connections from public networks, or only through private endpoints and trusted Microsoft services. The `Public network access` setting, `Enabled` or `Disabled`, selects between them.  **Prerequisites:** Give every client that needs data-plane access an approved private endpoint with private DNS resolution before disabling public network access.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: With public network access enabled, the HSM's data-plane endpoint is reachable from the internet, limited at most by an IP address allowlist and guarded otherwise only by Microsoft Entra authentication and local role assignments. A stolen token or an over-broad role assignment can then be used from anywhere to run cryptographic operations with the HSM's keys.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Clients that do not connect through a private endpoint lose data-plane access, including portal users listing keys from outside the private network. Managed HSM does not support virtual network service endpoints, so every client needs a private endpoint, which adds cost and network configuration.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: Complete the prerequisites in the Description before remediating.  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Managed HSM Pools`. 2. Click the name of a Managed HSM. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Networking`. 4. Click the `Public access` tab. 5. Under `Public network access`, click `Manage`. 6. Next to `Public network access`, select `Disable`. 7. Click `Save`. 8. Repeat steps 1-7 for each Managed HSM requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each Managed HSM requiring remediation, run the following command to disable public network access:  ``` az keyvault update-hsm --resource-group <resource-group> --hsm-name <hsm-name> --public-network-access Disabled ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each Managed HSM requiring remediation, run the following command to disable public network access:  ``` Update-AzKeyVaultManagedHsm -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <hsm-name> -PublicNetworkAccess Disabled ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Note:** Data-plane access is not required; Azure Resource Manager read access is sufficient.  **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Managed HSM Pools`. 2. Click the name of a Managed HSM. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Networking`. 4. Click the `Public access` tab. 5. Ensure that `Public network access` is set to `Disable`. 6. Repeat steps 1-5 for each Managed HSM.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list Managed HSMs:  ``` az keyvault list --resource-type hsm --query "[].{name:name, resourceGroup:resourceGroup}" --output table ```  For each Managed HSM, run the following command to get the public network access setting:  ``` az keyvault show --resource-group <resource-group> --hsm-name <hsm-name> --query properties.publicNetworkAccess --output tsv ```  Ensure that `Disabled` is returned.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Run the following command to list Managed HSMs:  ``` Get-AzKeyVaultManagedHsm ```  For each Managed HSM, run the following command to get the public network access setting:  ``` Get-AzKeyVaultManagedHsm -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <hsm-name> | Select-Object Name, PublicNetworkAccess ```  Ensure that `PublicNetworkAccess` is `Disabled`.
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: Disabling public network access does not suppress the trusted Microsoft services bypass; trusted services continue to reach the HSM without a private endpoint. The built-in Azure Policy '[Preview]: Azure Key Vault Managed HSM should disable public network access' evaluates the firewall default action, not this setting, so it is not cited as an audit method. The recommendation 'Ensure Private Endpoints are Used to Access Azure Key Vault Managed HSM' provides the private path this recommendation depends on.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, public network access is `Enabled` on a new Managed HSM.

Requirements.Description: Ensure Private Endpoints are Used to Access Azure Key Vault Managed HSM

Attributes.Description: A Managed HSM is reached through its public endpoint or through private endpoints that connect a virtual network to it over Azure Private Link. Each private endpoint connection is `Pending`, `Approved`, `Rejected`, or `Disconnected`, and only an `Approved` connection carries traffic.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Without a private endpoint, every client reaches the HSM's data plane over its public endpoint, so public network access cannot be disabled without cutting off every client; Managed HSM supports no virtual network service endpoints as an alternative. Key operations then cross public networks to an endpoint that any internet address can reach and probe.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Private endpoints are billed per hour and per gigabyte processed, and each client virtual network needs private DNS resolution for the HSM, which adds network configuration to every workload that uses it.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Note:** A private endpoint carries client traffic only when the private DNS zone `privatelink.managedhsm.azure.net` is linked to the client's virtual network and holds a record for the HSM, so configure that zone with each endpoint.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each Managed HSM requiring remediation, run the following command to create a private endpoint:  ``` az network private-endpoint create --resource-group <resource-group> --vnet-name <vnet-name> --subnet <subnet-name> --name <private-endpoint-name> --private-connection-resource-id <hsm-resource-id> --group-id managedhsm --connection-name <connection-name> --location <region> ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each Managed HSM requiring remediation, run the following commands to create a private endpoint:  ``` $hsm = Get-AzKeyVaultManagedHsm -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <hsm-name> $subnet = Get-AzVirtualNetwork -ResourceGroupName <vnet-resource-group> -Name <vnet-name> | Get-AzVirtualNetworkSubnetConfig -Name <subnet-name> $connection = New-AzPrivateLinkServiceConnection -Name <connection-name> -PrivateLinkServiceId $hsm.ResourceId -GroupId managedhsm New-AzPrivateEndpoint -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <private-endpoint-name> -Location <region> -Subnet $subnet -PrivateLinkServiceConnection $connection ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Note:** Data-plane access is not required; no Azure Portal method is given because Microsoft's Managed HSM private endpoint guide gives Azure CLI steps only.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list Managed HSMs:  ``` az keyvault list --resource-type hsm --query "[].{name:name, resourceGroup:resourceGroup}" --output table ```  For each Managed HSM, run the following command to list the status of its private endpoint connections:  ``` az keyvault private-endpoint-connection list --resource-group <resource-group> --hsm-name <hsm-name> --query "[].privateLinkServiceConnectionState.status" --output tsv ```  Ensure that at least one connection returns `Approved`.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Run the following command to list Managed HSMs:  ``` Get-AzKeyVaultManagedHsm ```  For each Managed HSM, run the following commands to list its private endpoint connections:  ``` $hsm = Get-AzKeyVaultManagedHsm -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <hsm-name> Get-AzPrivateEndpointConnection -PrivateLinkResourceId $hsm.ResourceId | Select-Object Name, @{Name='Status'; Expression={$_.PrivateLinkServiceConnectionState.Status}} ```  Ensure that at least one connection has the status `Approved`.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [59fee2f4-d439-4f1b-9b9a-982e1474bfd8](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2F59fee2f4-d439-4f1b-9b9a-982e1474bfd8) **- Name:** '[Preview]: Azure Key Vault Managed HSM should use private link'
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: Pair this recommendation with 'Ensure 'Public Network Access' is 'Disabled' for Azure Key Vault Managed HSM', which closes the public endpoint once private access is in place. A private endpoint created with the manual-request option stays `Pending` until it is approved. A private endpoint stops working if the HSM is deleted and later recovered, and must then be re-created. A Managed HSM supports up to 64 private endpoints.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, a Managed HSM has no private endpoint connections.

Requirements.Description: Ensure that the Expiration Date is Set for all Keys in Key Vaults using RBAC

Attributes.Description: Ensure that all Keys in Azure Key Vaults using Role Based Access Control (RBAC) have an expiration date set.  **Note:** The audit commands require data-plane access to each Key Vault in addition to the management-plane `Reader` role. Without data-plane access these commands return empty results silently.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: The Azure Key Vault enables users to store and use cryptographic keys within the Microsoft Azure environment. The `exp` (expiration date) attribute identifies the expiration date on or after which the key MUST NOT be used for encryption of new data, wrapping of new keys, and signing. By default, keys never expire. It is thus recommended that keys be rotated in the key vault and set an explicit expiration date for all keys to help enforce the key rotation. This ensures that the keys cannot be used beyond their assigned lifetimes.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Keys cannot be used beyond their assigned expiration dates respectively. Keys need to be rotated periodically wherever they are used.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Requisite RBAC Permissions for Keys - read section overview!**  Remediation Role = `Key Vault Crypto Officer`  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Key vaults`. 2. For each Key vault, under `Objects`, select `Keys`. 3. In the main pane, ensure that the status of the key(s) is `Enabled`. 4. Click on the Key without `Expiration date`. 5. Click the checkbox `Set expiration date` and set an appropriate `Expiration date` on the Key. 6. Click Apply.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  Update the `Expiration date` for the key using the below command:  ``` az keyvault key set-attributes --name <keyName> --vault-name <vaultName> --expires Y-m-d'T'H:M:S'Z' ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  ``` Set-AzKeyVaultKeyAttribute -VaultName <VaultName> -Name <KeyName> -Expires <DateTime> ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Requisite RBAC Permissions for Keys - read section overview!**  Audit Role = `Key Vault Crypto User`  **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Key vaults`. 2. For each Key vault, under `Objects` select, `Keys`. 3. In the main pane, ensure that the status of the key is `enabled`. 4. For each enabled key, ensure that an appropriate `Expiration date` is set.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Get a list of all the key vaults in your Azure environment by running the following command:  ``` az keyvault list ```  Then for each key vault listed ensure that the output of the below command contains Key ID (kid), enabled status as `true` and Expiration date (`expires`) is not `empty` or `null`:  ``` az keyvault key list --vault-name <VaultName> --query '[*].{"kid":kid,"enabled":attributes.enabled,"expires":attributes.expires}' ```  **Audit from PowerShell**  Retrieve a list of Azure Key Vaults:  ``` Get-AzKeyVault ```  For each Key vault run the following command to determine which vaults are configured to use RBAC.  ``` (Get-AzKeyVault -VaultName <Vault Name>).EnableRbacAuthorization ```  For each Key vault with the `EnableRbacAuthorization` setting set to `True`, run the following command.  ``` Get-AzKeyVaultKey -VaultName <Vault Name> | Where-Object { $_.Enabled -and -not $_.Expires } ```  This returns keys where `Expires` setting is not configured with a value and the `Enabled` setting is set to `True`.  **To audit at scale** Enumerates ALL Key Vaults in the CURRENT subscription context only. Does NOT cover the entire tenant unless you loop through all subscriptions. Uses ARM (`Get-AzResource`) to reliably read `enableRbacAuthorization`.  ``` $vaults = Get-AzResource -ResourceType "Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults" | ForEach-Object { $kv = Get-AzResource -ResourceId $_.ResourceId -ExpandProperties if ($kv.Properties.enableRbacAuthorization -eq $true) { [PSCustomObject]@{ VaultName = $kv.Name ResourceGroup = $kv.ResourceGroupName EnableRbacAuthorization = $kv.Properties.enableRbacAuthorization SubscriptionId = $kv.SubscriptionId } } } ```  Retrieves ALL keys in EACH RBAC-enabled vault in the CURRENT subscription. This can be very heavy in large environments (no filtering at API level). Returns ONLY violations: enabled secrets WITHOUT expiration.  ``` foreach ($vault in $vaults) { Get-AzKeyVaultKey -VaultName $vault.VaultName | Where-Object { $_.Enabled -eq $true -and $_.Expires -eq $null } | Select-Object @{Name="VaultName";Expression={$vault.VaultName}}, Name, Enabled, Expires } ```  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [152b15f7-8e1f-4c1f-ab71-8c010ba5dbc0](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2F152b15f7-8e1f-4c1f-ab71-8c010ba5dbc0) **- Name:** 'Key Vault keys should have an expiration date'
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, keys do not expire.

Requirements.Description: Ensure that the Expiration Date is set for All Keys in Key Vaults using access policies (legacy)

Attributes.Description: Ensure that all Keys in Azure Key Vaults with access policies have an expiration date set.  **Note:** Using access policies is a legacy method. For improved security, use the Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) permission model instead of access policies when managing Azure Key Vault. RBAC restricts permission management to only the `Owner` and `User Access Administrator` roles, ensuring a clear separation between security and administrative tasks. With the Access Policy permission model, users with the `Contributor`, `Key Vault Contributor`, or any role that includes `Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/write` permissions can grant themselves data plane access by configuring a Key Vault access policy. This can result in unauthorized access and management of your key vaults, keys, secrets, and certificates. To reduce this risk, limit `Contributor` role access to key vaults when using the Access Policy model.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Azure Key Vault enables users to store and use cryptographic keys within the Microsoft Azure environment. The `exp` (expiration date) attribute identifies the expiration date on or after which the key MUST NOT be used for a cryptographic operation. By default, keys never expire. It is thus recommended that keys be rotated in the key vault and set an explicit expiration date for all keys. This ensures that the keys cannot be used beyond their assigned lifetimes.

For each Key vault, under `Objects`, select `Secrets`. 3. In the main pane, ensure that the status of the secret is `Enabled`. 4. For each enabled secret, ensure that an appropriate `Expiration date` is set.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Ensure that the output of the below command contains ID (id), enabled status as `true` and Expiration date (`expires`) is not `empty` or `null`:  ``` az keyvault secret list --vault-name <KEYVAULTNAME> --query '[*].{"kid":kid,"enabled":attributes.enabled,"expires":attributes.expires}' ```  **Audit from PowerShell**  Retrieve a list of Key Vaults:  ``` Get-AzKeyVault ```  For each Key vault, run the following command to determine which vaults are configured to use RBAC:  ``` (Get-AzKeyVault -VaultName <Vault Name>).EnableRbacAuthorization ```  For each Key vault with the `EnableRbacAuthorization` setting set to `True`, run the following command:  ``` Get-AzKeyVaultSecret -VaultName <Vault Name> | Where-Object { $_.Enabled -and -not $_.Expires } ```  This returns secrets where `Expires` setting is not configured with a value and the `Enabled` setting is set to `True`.  **To audit at scale** Enumerates ALL Key Vaults in the CURRENT subscription context only. Does NOT cover the entire tenant unless you loop through all subscriptions. Uses ARM (`Get-AzResource`) to reliably read `enableRbacAuthorization`.  ``` $vaults = Get-AzResource -ResourceType "Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults" | ForEach-Object { $kv = Get-AzResource -ResourceId $_.ResourceId -ExpandProperties if ($kv.Properties.enableRbacAuthorization -eq $true) { [PSCustomObject]@{ VaultName = $kv.Name ResourceGroup = $kv.ResourceGroupName EnableRbacAuthorization = $kv.Properties.enableRbacAuthorization SubscriptionId = $kv.SubscriptionId } } } ```  Retrieves ALL secrets in EACH RBAC-enabled vault in the CURRENT subscription. Returns ONLY violations: enabled secrets WITHOUT expiration.  ``` foreach ($vault in $vaults) { Get-AzKeyVaultSecret -VaultName $vault.VaultName | Where-Object { $_.Enabled -eq $true -and $_.Expires -eq $null } | Select-Object @{Name="VaultName";Expression={$vault.VaultName}}, Name, Enabled, Expires } ```  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure. Requirements.Description: Ensure that the Expiration Date is set for All Secrets in Key Vaults using access policies (legacy)

Attributes.Description: Ensure that all Secrets in Azure Key Vaults with access policies have an expiration date set.  **Note:** Using access policies is a legacy method. This can result in unauthorized access and management of your key vaults, keys, secrets, and certificates. Attributes.Description: Restrict the validity period of certificates stored in Azure Key Vault to 12 months or less.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Limiting certificate validity reduces the risk of misuse if compromised and helps ensure timely renewal, improving security and reliability.
