Requirements.Description: Ensure Automatic Key Rotation is Enabled within Azure Key Vault

Attributes.Description: Automated cryptographic key rotation in Key Vault allows users to configure Key Vault to automatically generate a new key version at a specified frequency. A key rotation policy can be defined for each individual key.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Automatic key rotation reduces risk by ensuring that keys are rotated without manual intervention.  Azure and NIST recommend that keys be rotated every two years or less. Refer to 'Table 1: Suggested cryptoperiods for key types' on page 46 of the following document for more information: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-57pt1r5.pdf.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: There is an additional cost for each scheduled key rotation.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Requisite Permissions - read section overview!**  RBAC Role = `Key Vault Crypto Officer`  Access policy permission = Rotation Policy Operations: `Set Rotation Policy`  **Note:** Azure CLI and PowerShell use the ISO8601 duration format for time spans. The format is `P<timespanInISO8601Format>(Y,M,D)`. The leading P is required and is referred to as `period`. The `(Y,M,D)` are for the duration of Year, Month, and Day, respectively. A time frame of 2 years, 2 months, 2 days would be `P2Y2M2D`. For Azure CLI and PowerShell, it is easiest to supply the policy flags in a `.json file`, for example:  ``` { "lifetimeActions": [ { "trigger": { "timeAfterCreate": "P<timespanInISO8601Format>(Y,M,D)", "timeBeforeExpiry" : null }, "action": { "type": "Rotate" } }, { "trigger": { "timeBeforeExpiry" : "P<timespanInISO8601Format>(Y,M,D)" }, "action": { "type": "Notify" } } ], "attributes": { "expiryTime": "P<timespanInISO8601Format>(Y,M,D)" } } ```  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Key Vaults`. 2. Select a Key Vault. 3. Under `Objects`, select `Keys`. 4. Select a key. 5. From the top row, select `Rotation policy`. 6. Select an appropriate `Expiry time`. 7. Set `Enable auto rotation` to `Enabled`. 8. Set an appropriate `Rotation option` and `Rotation time`. 9. Optionally, set a `Notification time`. 10. Click `Save`. 11. Repeat steps 1-10 for each Key Vault and Key.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  Run the following command for each key to enable automatic rotation:  ``` az keyvault key rotation-policy update --vault-name <vault-name> --name <key-name> --value <path/to/policy.json> ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  Run the following command for each key to enable automatic rotation:  ``` Set-AzKeyVaultKeyRotationPolicy -VaultName <vault-name> -Name <key-name> -PolicyPath <path/to/policy.json> ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Requisite Permissions - read section overview!**  RBAC Role = `Key Vault Reader`  Access policy permission = Rotation Policy Operations: `Get Rotation Policy`  **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Key Vaults`. 2. Select a Key Vault. 3. Under `Objects`, select `Keys`. 4. Select a key. 5. From the top row, select `Rotation policy`. 6. Verify that `Enable auto rotation` is set to `Enabled`. 7. Verify that `Rotation time` is set to an appropriate value. 8. Repeat steps 1-7 for each Key Vault and key.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command:  ``` az keyvault key rotation-policy show --vault-name <vault-name> --name <key-name> ```  Verify that `lifetimeActions` contains an action of type `Rotate` whose trigger sets `timeAfterCreate` or `timeBeforeExpiry` to an appropriate value. A `timeBeforeExpiry` trigger also requires an `expiryTime` in the policy attributes.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Run the following command:  ``` Get-AzKeyVaultKeyRotationPolicy -VaultName <vault-name> -Name <key-name> ```  Verify that `LifetimeActions` contains an action of `Rotate` with `TimeAfterCreate` or `TimeBeforeExpiry` set to an appropriate value. A `TimeBeforeExpiry` trigger also requires `ExpiresIn` to be set.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [d8cf8476-a2ec-4916-896e-992351803c44](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2Fd8cf8476-a2ec-4916-896e-992351803c44) **- Name:** 'Keys should have a rotation policy ensuring that their rotation is scheduled within the specified number of days after creation.'
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, automatic key rotation is not enabled.

Requirements.Description: Ensure 'Purge protection' is Set to 'Enabled'

Attributes.Description: Key vaults contain object keys, secrets, and certificates. Deletion of a key vault can cause immediate data loss or loss of security functions (authentication, validation, verification, non-repudiation, etc.) supported by the key vault objects.  It is recommended the key vault be made recoverable by enabling the "purge protection" function. This is to prevent the loss of encrypted data, including storage accounts, SQL databases, and/or dependent services provided by key vault objects (keys, secrets, certificates, etc.).  **Note:** In February 2025, Microsoft enabled soft delete protection on all key vaults. Users can no longer opt out of or turn off soft delete.  **Warning:** A current limitation is that role assignments disappear when a key vault is deleted. All role assignments will need to be recreated after recovery.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Users may accidentally run delete/purge commands on a key vault, or an attacker or malicious user may do so deliberately in order to cause disruption. Deleting or purging a key vault leads to immediate data loss, as keys encrypting data and secrets/certificates allowing access/services will become inaccessible.  Enabling purge protection ensures that even if a key vault is deleted, the key vault and its objects remain recoverable during the configurable retention period. If no action is taken, the key vault and its objects will be purged once the retention period elapses.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Once purge protection is enabled for a key vault, it cannot be disabled.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Requisite Permissions - read section overview!**  Data-plane access not required. Can be audited and remediated with Azure Resource Manager permissions.  **Note:** Once enabled, purge protection cannot be disabled.  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Key Vaults`. 2. Click the name of a key vault. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Properties`. 4. Select the radio button next to `Enable purge protection (enforce a mandatory retention period for deleted vaults and vault objects)`. 5. Click `Save`. 6. Repeat steps 1-5 for each key vault requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each key vault requiring remediation, run the following command to enable purge protection:  ``` az resource update --resource-group <resource-group> --name <key-vault> --resource-type "Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults" --set properties.enablePurgeProtection=true ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each key vault requiring remediation, run the following command to enable purge protection:  ``` Update-AzKeyVault -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -VaultName <key-vault> -EnablePurgeProtection ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Requisite Permissions - read section overview!**  Data-plane access not required. Can be audited and remediated with Azure Resource Manager permissions.  **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Key Vaults`. 2. Click the name of a key vault. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Properties`. 4. Next to `Purge protection`, ensure that `Enable purge protection (enforce a mandatory retention period for deleted vaults and vault objects)` is selected. 5. Repeat steps 1-4 for each key vault.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list key vaults:  ``` az resource list --query "[?type=='Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults']" ```  For each key vault, run the following command to get the purge protection setting:  ``` az resource show --resource-group <resource-group> --name <key-vault> --resource-type "Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults" --query properties.enablePurgeProtection ```  Ensure that `true` is returned.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Run the following command to list key vaults:  ``` Get-AzKeyVault ```  For each key vault, run the following command to get the key vault details:  ``` Get-AzKeyVault -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -VaultName <key-vault> ```  Ensure `Purge Protection Enabled?` is set to `True`.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [0b60c0b2-2dc2-4e1c-b5c9-abbed971de53](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2F0b60c0b2-2dc2-4e1c-b5c9-abbed971de53) **- Name:** 'Key vaults should have deletion protection enabled'
Attributes.DefaultValue: Purge protection is disabled by default.

Requirements.Description: Ensure that Role Based Access Control for Azure Key Vault is Enabled

Attributes.Description: The recommended way to access Key Vaults is to use the Azure Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) permissions model.  Azure RBAC is an authorization system built on Azure Resource Manager that provides fine-grained access management of Azure resources. It allows users to manage Key, Secret, and Certificate permissions. It provides one place to manage all permissions across all key vaults.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: The new RBAC permissions model for Key Vaults enables a much finer grained access control for key vault secrets, keys, certificates, etc., than the vault access policy. This in turn will permit the use of privileged identity management over these roles, thus securing the key vaults with JIT Access management.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Implementation needs to be properly designed from the ground up, as this is a fundamental change to the way key vaults are accessed/managed. Changing permissions to key vaults will result in loss of service as permissions are re-applied. For the least amount of downtime, map your current groups and users to their corresponding permission needs.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Requisite Permissions - read section overview!**  Data-plane access not required. Can be audited and remediated with Azure Resource Manager permissions.  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  Key Vaults can be configured to use `Azure role-based access control` on creation.  For existing Key Vaults:  1. From Azure Home open the Portal Menu in the top left corner 2. Select `Key Vaults` 3. Select a Key Vault to audit 4. Under `Settings` select `Access configuration` 5. Set the Permission model radio button to `Azure role-based access control`, taking note of the warning message 6. Click `Save` 7. Select `Access Control (IAM)` 8. Select the `Role Assignments` tab 9. Reapply permissions as needed to groups or users  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  To enable RBAC Authorization for each Key Vault, run the following Azure CLI command:  ``` az keyvault update --resource-group <resource_group> --name <vault_name> --enable-rbac-authorization true ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  To enable RBAC authorization on each Key Vault, run the following PowerShell command:  ``` Update-AzKeyVault -ResourceGroupName <resource_group> -VaultName <vault_name> -EnableRbacAuthorization $True ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Requisite Permissions - read section overview!**  Data-plane access not required. Can be audited and remediated with Azure Resource Manager permissions.  **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. From Azure Home open the Portal Menu in the top left corner. 2. Select `Key Vaults`. 3. Select a Key Vault to audit. 4. Under `Settings` select `Access configuration`. 5. Ensure the Permission Model radio button is set to `Azure role-based access control`.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command for each Key Vault in each Resource Group:  ``` az keyvault show --resource-group <resource_group> --name <vault_name> ```  Ensure the `enableRbacAuthorization` setting is set to `true` within the output of the above command.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Run the following PowerShell command:  ``` Get-AzKeyVault -Vaultname <vault_name> -ResourceGroupName <resource_group> ```  Ensure the `Enabled For RBAC Authorization` setting is set to `True`  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [12d4fa5e-1f9f-4c21-97a9-b99b3c6611b5](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2F12d4fa5e-1f9f-4c21-97a9-b99b3c6611b5) **- Name:** 'Azure Key Vault should use RBAC permission model'
Attributes.DefaultValue: The default value for Access control in Key Vaults is Vault Policy.

Requirements.Description: Ensure the Default Network Access Rule for Key Vaults is Set to Deny

Attributes.Description: A key vault accepts data-plane connections from all networks, only from allowed virtual networks and IP addresses, or only through private endpoints. The `Allow access from` setting selects between `Allow public access from all networks`, `Allow public access from specific virtual networks and IP addresses`, and `Disable public access`.  **Prerequisites:** Add a virtual network rule, an IP address rule, or a private endpoint for every client that needs data-plane access before setting the default action to deny.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: With the default network access rule set to allow, the vault's data plane accepts connections from any internet address, and its virtual network and IP address rules have no effect, so the vault can appear network-restricted while it is not. A leaked token or a misassigned role can then be used against its keys, secrets, and certificates from anywhere.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Clients outside the allowed virtual networks and IP address ranges lose data-plane access, including portal users listing keys or secrets from an unlisted address. Azure services that are not on the trusted services list need a private endpoint or an allowed network, and trusted services need the `Allow trusted Microsoft services to bypass this firewall` exception.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: Complete the prerequisites in the Description before remediating.  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Key vaults`. 2. Click the name of a key vault. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Networking`. 4. On the `Firewalls and virtual networks` tab, next to `Allow access from:`, select `Allow public access from specific virtual networks and IP addresses`. 5. Add the virtual networks and IP addresses that require access. 6. Click `Apply`. 7. Repeat steps 1-6 for each key vault requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each key vault requiring remediation, run the following command to set the default network action to deny:  ``` az keyvault update --resource-group <resource-group> --name <key-vault> --default-action Deny ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each key vault requiring remediation, run the following command to set the default network action to deny:  ``` Update-AzKeyVaultNetworkRuleSet -VaultName <key-vault> -DefaultAction Deny ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Note:** Data-plane access is not required; Azure Resource Manager read access is sufficient.  **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Key vaults`. 2. Click the name of a key vault. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Networking`. 4. On the `Firewalls and virtual networks` tab, ensure that `Allow access from:` is set to `Allow public access from specific virtual networks and IP addresses` or `Disable public access`. 5. Repeat steps 1-4 for each key vault.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list key vaults:  ``` az keyvault list --resource-type vault --query "[].{name:name, resourceGroup:resourceGroup}" --output table ```  For each key vault, run the following command:  ``` az keyvault show --resource-group <resource-group> --name <key-vault> --query "{publicNetworkAccess:properties.publicNetworkAccess, defaultAction:properties.networkAcls.defaultAction}" ```  Ensure that `defaultAction` is `Deny`, or that `publicNetworkAccess` is `Disabled`. An empty `defaultAction` means that all networks are allowed.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Run the following command to list key vaults:  ``` Get-AzKeyVault ```  For each key vault, run the following commands:  ``` $vault = Get-AzKeyVault -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -VaultName <key-vault> $vault.PublicNetworkAccess $vault.NetworkAcls.DefaultAction ```  Ensure that the default action is `Deny`, or that public network access is `Disabled`.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [55615ac9-af46-4a59-874e-391cc3dfb490](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2F55615ac9-af46-4a59-874e-391cc3dfb490) **- Name:** 'Azure Key Vault should have firewall enabled or public network access disabled'
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: The recommendation 'Ensure Public Network Access is Disabled' is the stronger setting: a vault that meets it also meets this recommendation, which covers vaults that keep public network access enabled. Key Vault firewall rules apply only to data-plane operations. IP address rules accept public IPv4 addresses and ranges only. A vault associated with a network security perimeter reports public network access as secured by perimeter, and it passes this recommendation and the cited Azure Policy only when its default action is also `Deny`.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, a new key vault allows public access from all networks.

Requirements.Description: Ensure Public Network Access is Disabled

Attributes.Description: Disable public network access to prevent exposure to the internet and reduce the risk of unauthorized access. Use private endpoints to securely manage access within trusted networks.  When a private endpoint is configured on a key vault, connections from Azure resources within the same subnet will use its private IP address. However, network traffic from the public internet can still connect to the key vault's public endpoint (mykeyvault.vault.azure.net) using its public IP address unless public network access is disabled.  Disabling public network access removes the vault's public endpoint from Azure public DNS, reducing its exposure to the public internet. With a private endpoint configured, network traffic will use the vault's private endpoint IP address for all requests (mykeyvault.vault.privatelink.azure.net).
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Disabling public network access improves security by ensuring that a service is not exposed on the public internet.  Removing a point of interconnection from the internet edge to your key vault can strengthen the network security boundary of your system and reduce the risk of exposing the control plane or vault objects to untrusted clients.  Although Azure resources are never truly isolated from the public internet, disabling the public endpoint removes a line of sight from the public internet and increases the effort required for an attack.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: **Note:** Prior to disabling public network access, it is strongly recommended that, for each key vault, either:  - virtual network integration is completed  OR  - private endpoints/links are set up as described in **"Ensure Private Endpoints are used to access Azure Key Vault."**  Disabling public network access restricts access to the service. This enhances security but will require the configuration of a virtual network and/or private endpoints for any services or users needing access within trusted networks.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Requisite Permissions - read section overview!**  Data-plane access not required. Can be audited and remediated with Azure Resource Manager permissions.  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Key vaults`. 2. Click the name of a key vault. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Networking`. 4. Under `Firewalls and virtual networks`, next to `Allow access from:`, click the radio button next to `Disable public access`. 5. Click `Apply`. 6. Repeat steps 1-5 for each key vault requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each key vault requiring remediation, run the following command to disable public network access:  ``` az keyvault update --resource-group <resource-group> --name <key-vault> --public-network-access Disabled ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each key vault requiring remediation, run the following command to disable public network access:  ``` Update-AzKeyVault -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -VaultName <vault-name> -PublicNetworkAccess "Disabled" ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Requisite Permissions - read section overview!**  Data-plane access not required. Can be audited and remediated with Azure Resource Manager permissions.  **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Key vaults`. 2. Click the name of a key vault. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Networking`. 4. Under `Firewalls and virtual networks`, ensure that `Allow access from:` is set to `Disable public access`. 5. Repeat steps 1-4 for each key vault.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list key vaults:  ``` az keyvault list ```  For each key vault, run the following command to get the public network access setting:  ``` az keyvault show --resource-group <resource-group> --name <key-vault> --query properties.publicNetworkAccess ```  Ensure that "Disabled" is returned.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Run the following command to list key vaults:  ``` Get-AzKeyVault ```  Run the following command to get the key vault in a resource group with a given name:  ``` $vault = Get-AzKeyVault -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <key-vault> ```  Run the following command to get the public network access setting for the key vault:  ``` $vault.PublicNetworkAccess ```  Ensure that `Disabled` is returned.  Repeat for each key vault.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [405c5871-3e91-4644-8a63-58e19d68ff5b](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2F405c5871-3e91-4644-8a63-58e19d68ff5b) **- Name:** 'Azure Key Vault should disable public network access'
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: This recommendation is based on the Common Reference Recommendation `Ensure public network access is Disabled`, from the `Common Reference Recommendations > Networking > Virtual Networks (VNets)` section.
Attributes.DefaultValue: Public network access is enabled by default.

Requirements.Description: Ensure Private Endpoints are Used to Access Azure Key Vault

Attributes.Description: Use private endpoints to allow clients and services to securely access data located over a network via an encrypted Private Link. To do this, the private endpoint uses an IP address from the VNet for each service. Network traffic between disparate services securely traverses encrypted over the VNet. This VNet can also link addressing space, extending your network and accessing resources on it. Similarly, it can be a tunnel through public networks to connect remote infrastructures together. This creates further security through segmenting network traffic and preventing outside sources from accessing it.  Private endpoints will secure network traffic from Azure Key Vault to the resources requesting secrets and keys.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Securing traffic between services through encryption protects the data from easy interception and reading.  Private endpoints will keep network requests to Azure Key Vault limited to the endpoints attached to the resources that are whitelisted to communicate with each other. Assigning the Key Vault to a network without an endpoint will allow other resources on that network to view all traffic from the Key Vault to its destination. In spite of the complexity in configuration, this is recommended for high security secrets.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: If an Azure Virtual Network is not implemented correctly, this may result in the loss of critical network traffic.  Private endpoints are charged per hour of use. Refer to https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/private-link/ and https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/calculator/ to estimate potential costs.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Requisite Permissions - read section overview!**  Data-plane access not required. Can be audited and remediated with Azure Resource Manager permissions.  **Please see the additional information about the requirements needed before starting this remediation procedure.**  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. From Azure Home open the Portal Menu in the top left. 2. Select `Key Vaults`. 3. Select a Key Vault to audit. 4. Select `Networking` in the left column. 5. Select `Private endpoint connections` from the top row. 6. Select `+ Create`. 7. Select the subscription the Key Vault is within, and other desired configuration. 8. Select `Next`. 9. For resource type select `Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults`. 10. Select the Key Vault to associate the Private Endpoint with. 11. Select `Next`. 12. In the `Virtual Networking` field, select the network to assign the Endpoint. 13. Select other configuration options as desired, including an existing or new application security group. 14. Select `Next`. 15. Select the private DNS the Private Endpoints will use. 16. Select `Next`. 17. Optionally add `Tags`. 18. Select `Next : Review + Create`. 19. Review the information and select `Create`. Follow the Audit Procedure to determine if it has successfully applied. 20. Repeat steps 3-19 for each Key Vault.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  1. To create an endpoint, run the following command:  ``` az network private-endpoint create --resource-group <resourceGroup --vnet-name <vnetName> --subnet <subnetName> --name <PrivateEndpointName>  --private-connection-resource-id "/subscriptions/<AZURE SUBSCRIPTION ID>/resourceGroups/<resourceGroup>/providers/Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/<keyVaultName>" --group-ids vault --connection-name <privateLinkConnectionName> --location <azureRegion> --manual-request ```  2. To manually approve the endpoint request, run the following command:  ``` az keyvault private-endpoint-connection approve --resource-group <resourceGroup> --vault-name <keyVaultName> --name <privateLinkName> ```  3. Determine the Private Endpoint's IP address to connect the Key Vault to the Private DNS you have previously created: 4. Look for the property networkInterfaces then id; the value must be placed in the variable <privateEndpointNIC> within step 7.  ``` az network private-endpoint show -g <resourceGroupName> -n <privateEndpointName> ```  5. Look for the property networkInterfaces then id; the value must be placed on <privateEndpointNIC> in step 7.  ``` az network nic show --ids <privateEndpointName> ```  6. Create a Private DNS record within the DNS Zone you created for the Private Endpoint:  ``` az network private-dns record-set a add-record -g <resourcecGroupName> -z "privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net" -n <keyVaultName> -a <privateEndpointNIC> ```  7. nslookup the private endpoint to determine if the DNS record is correct:  ``` nslookup <keyVaultName>.vault.azure.net nslookup <keyVaultName>.privatelink.vaultcore.azure.n ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Requisite Permissions - read section overview!**  Data-plane access not required. Can be audited and remediated with Azure Resource Manager permissions.  **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. From Azure Home open the Portal Menu in the top left. 2. Select `Key Vaults`. 3. Select a Key Vault to audit. 4. Select `Networking` in the left column. 5. Select `Private endpoint connections` from the top row. 6. View if there is an endpoint attached.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command within a subscription for each Key Vault you wish to audit.  ``` az keyvault show --name <keyVaultName> ```  Ensure that `privateEndpointConnections` is not `null`.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Run the following command within a subscription for each Key Vault you wish to audit.  ``` Get-AzPrivateEndpointConnection -PrivateLinkResourceId '/subscriptions/<subscriptionNumber>/resourceGroups/<resourceGroup>/providers/Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/<keyVaultName>/' ```  Ensure that the response contains details of a private endpoint.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [a6abeaec-4d90-4a02-805f-6b26c4d3fbe9](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2Fa6abeaec-4d90-4a02-805f-6b26c4d3fbe9) **- Name:** 'Azure Key Vaults should use private link'
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: This recommendation assumes that you have created a Resource Group containing a Virtual Network that the services are already associated with and configured private DNS. A Bastion on the virtual network is also required, and the service to which you are connecting must already have a Private Endpoint. For information concerning the installation of these services, please see the attached documentation.  Microsoft's own documentation lists the requirements as: A Key Vault. An Azure virtual network. A subnet in the virtual network. Owner or contributor permissions for both the Key Vault and the virtual network.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, Private Endpoints are not created for services.

Requirements.Description: Ensure an Azure Bastion Host Exists

Attributes.Description: The Azure Bastion service allows secure remote access to Azure Virtual Machines over the Internet without exposing remote access protocol ports and services directly to the Internet. The Azure Bastion service provides this access using TLS over 443/TCP, and subscribes to hardened configurations within an organization's Azure Active Directory service.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: The Azure Bastion service allows organizations a more secure means of accessing Azure Virtual Machines over the Internet without assigning public IP addresses to those Virtual Machines. The Azure Bastion service provides Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) and Secure Shell (SSH) access to Virtual Machines using TLS within a web browser, thus preventing organizations from opening up 3389/TCP and 22/TCP to the Internet on Azure Virtual Machines. Additional benefits of the Bastion service includes Multi-Factor Authentication, Conditional Access Policies, and any other hardening measures configured within Azure Active Directory using a central point of access.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: The Azure Bastion service incurs additional costs and requires a specific virtual network configuration. The `Standard` tier offers additional configuration options compared to the `Basic` tier and may incur additional costs for those added features.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Click on `Bastions` 2. Select the `Subscription` 3. Select the `Resource group` 4. Type a `Name` for the new Bastion host 5. Select a `Region` 6. Choose `Standard` next to `Tier` 7. Use the slider to set the `Instance count` 8. Select the `Virtual network` or `Create new` 9. Select the `Subnet` named `AzureBastionSubnet`. Create a `Subnet` named `AzureBastionSubnet` using a `/26` CIDR range if it doesn't already exist. 10. Select the appropriate `Public IP address` option. 11. If `Create new` is selected for the `Public IP address` option, provide a `Public IP address name`. 12. If `Use existing` is selected for `Public IP address` option, select an IP address from `Choose public IP address` 13. Click `Next: Tags >` 14. Configure the appropriate `Tags` 15. Click `Next: Advanced >` 16. Select the appropriate `Advanced` options 17. Click `Next: Review + create >` 18. Click `Create`  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  ``` az network bastion create --location <location> --name <name of bastion host> --public-ip-address <public IP address name or ID> --resource-group <resource group name or ID> --vnet-name <virtual network containing subnet called "AzureBastionSubnet"> --scale-units <integer> --sku Standard [--disable-copy-paste true|false] [--enable-ip-connect true|false] [--enable-tunneling true|false] ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  Create the appropriate `Virtual network` settings and `Public IP Address` settings.  ``` $subnetName = "AzureBastionSubnet" $subnet = New-AzVirtualNetworkSubnetConfig -Name $subnetName -AddressPrefix <IP address range in CIDR notation making sure to use a /26> $virtualNet = New-AzVirtualNetwork -Name <virtual network name> -ResourceGroupName <resource group name> -Location <location> -AddressPrefix <IP address range in CIDR notation> -Subnet $subnet $publicip = New-AzPublicIpAddress -ResourceGroupName <resource group name> -Name <public IP address name> -Location <location> -AllocationMethod Dynamic -Sku Standard ```  Create the `Azure Bastion` service using the information within the created variables from above.  ``` New-AzBastion -ResourceGroupName <resource group name> -Name <bastion name> -PublicIpAddress $publicip -VirtualNetwork $virtualNet -Sku "Standard" -ScaleUnit <integer> ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Click on `Bastions` 2. Ensure there is at least one `Bastion` host listed under the `Name` column  **Audit from Azure CLI**  ``` az network bastion list --subscription <subscription ID> ```  Ensure the output of the above command is not empty.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Retrieve the `Bastion` host(s) information for a specific `Resource Group`  ``` Get-AzBastion -ResourceGroupName <resource group name> ```  Ensure the output of the above command is not empty.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, the Azure Bastion service is not configured.

Requirements.Description: Ensure 'Shareable Link' is Disabled on Azure Bastion Hosts

Attributes.Description: Shareable Link lets anyone holding a Bastion-generated URL reach a virtual machine's RDP or SSH sign-in without signing in to the Azure portal. Each Standard or Premium Bastion host has `Shareable Link` `Enabled` or `Disabled`; Basic and Developer hosts lack the feature and are out of scope.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: A shareable link exposes a virtual machine's RDP or SSH sign-in to anyone who obtains the URL, with no Microsoft Entra ID authentication, Conditional Access, or Azure role assignment in front of it. A leaked or forwarded link leaves only the virtual machine's local credentials between an attacker and an interactive session until the link expires or is deleted.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Users who connect through shareable links must instead connect through the Azure portal or a native client, signed in with a Microsoft Entra ID identity that holds the Reader roles Azure Bastion requires.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Bastions`. 2. Click the name of a `Standard` or `Premium` Bastion host. 3. Click `Configuration`. 4. Clear the `Shareable Link` check box. 5. Click `Apply`. 6. Repeat steps 1-5 for each Bastion host requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each Bastion host requiring remediation, run the following command to disable Shareable Link:  ``` az network bastion update --resource-group <resource-group> --name <bastion-host> --shareable-link false ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each Bastion host requiring remediation, run the following commands to disable Shareable Link:  ``` $bastion = Get-AzBastion -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <bastion-host> Set-AzBastion -InputObject $bastion -EnableShareableLink $false -Force ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Note:** No built-in Azure Policy definition evaluates the Shareable Link setting, so this recommendation has no Azure Policy method.  **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Bastions`. 2. Click the name of a Bastion host. 3. Click `Configuration`. 4. Confirm `Tier` is `Standard` or `Premium`; `Basic` and `Developer` hosts are out of scope. 5. Ensure `Shareable Link` is not selected. 6. Repeat steps 1-5 for each Bastion host.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  List the SKU and Shareable Link setting of every Bastion host:  ``` az network bastion list --query "[].{Name:name, ResourceGroup:resourceGroup, Sku:sku.name, ShareableLink:enableShareableLink}" --output table ```  Ensure no `Standard` or `Premium` host returns `True` for `ShareableLink`; `False` or an empty value is compliant.  **Audit from PowerShell**  List the SKU and Shareable Link setting of every Bastion host:  ``` Get-AzBastion | Select-Object Name, ResourceGroupName, @{n='Sku'; e={$_.Sku.Name}}, EnableShareableLink ```  Ensure no `Standard` or `Premium` host returns `True` for `EnableShareableLink`; `False` or an empty value is compliant.
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: Microsoft documentation does not state whether disabling the feature deletes shareable links that already exist. Delete existing links on the host's `Shareable links` page before disabling the feature, so that none become usable again if the feature is later re-enabled. Bastion configuration updates take about 10 minutes to apply.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, `Shareable Link` is `Disabled` on a new Bastion host.

Requirements.Description: Ensure Azure DDoS Protection is Enabled on Public IP Addresses

Attributes.Description: A public IP address is covered by Azure DDoS Protection through IP Protection, enabled on the address, or Network Protection, inherited from its virtual network. Its protection mode is `Enabled`, `VirtualNetworkInherited` or `Disabled`. Addresses DDoS Protection does not support, such as those on a NAT gateway, are out of scope.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Without IP Protection or Network Protection, a public IP address relies only on Azure DDoS infrastructure protection, whose mitigation thresholds are set for the platform rather than the application. Attack traffic below those thresholds can still exhaust the bandwidth, connections, or compute behind the address, and no attack telemetry, alerting, or mitigation report is produced.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: DDoS IP Protection is billed per protected public IP address. DDoS Network Protection is a fixed monthly plan that includes 100 public IP resources, with additional resources billed individually, and costs less above about 15 resources. IP Protection does not include DDoS Rapid Response support, cost protection, or the Web Application Firewall discount.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Note:** IP Protection requires a Standard SKU public IP address. A Basic SKU address, or an address from a public IP prefix linked to a public load balancer frontend, can be protected only through DDoS Network Protection on its virtual network.  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Public IP addresses`. 2. Click the name of a public IP address. 3. In the `Overview` pane, select the `Properties` tab, then click `DDoS protection`. 4. Under `Protection type`, select `IP`. 5. Click `Save`. 6. Repeat steps 1-5 for each public IP address requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each public IP address requiring remediation, run the following command to enable DDoS IP Protection:  ``` az network public-ip update --resource-group <resource-group> --name <public-ip-address> --ddos-protection-mode Enabled ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each public IP address requiring remediation, run the following commands to enable DDoS IP Protection:  ``` $publicIp = Get-AzPublicIpAddress -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <public-ip-address> $publicIp.DdosSettings.ProtectionMode = 'Enabled' Set-AzPublicIpAddress -PublicIpAddress $publicIp ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Note:** Exclude public IP addresses that Azure DDoS Protection does not support, such as those attached to a NAT gateway.  **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Public IP addresses`. 2. Click the name of a public IP address. 3. In the `Overview` pane, select the `Properties` tab, then click `DDoS protection`. 4. Ensure `Protection status` shows that the public IP address is protected. 5. Repeat steps 1-4 for each public IP address.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list the DDoS protection mode of each public IP address:  ``` az network public-ip list --query "[].{Name:name, ResourceGroup:resourceGroup, ProtectionMode:ddosSettings.protectionMode}" --output table ```  A value of `Enabled` means the address is protected directly. For any other or empty value, run the following command:  ``` az network public-ip ddos-protection show --resource-group <resource-group> --name <public-ip-address> --query isWorkloadProtected ```  Ensure `True` is returned.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Run the following command to list the DDoS protection mode of each public IP address:  ``` Get-AzPublicIpAddress | Select-Object Name, ResourceGroupName, @{Name='ProtectionMode'; Expression={$_.DdosSettings.ProtectionMode}} ```  A value of `Enabled` means the address is protected directly. For any other or empty value, run the following command:  ``` (Invoke-AzRestMethod -Method POST -Path "/subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/<resource-group>/providers/Microsoft.Network/publicIPAddresses/<public-ip-address>/ddosProtectionStatus?api-version=2026-01-01" -WaitForCompletion).Content | ConvertFrom-Json | Select-Object isWorkloadProtected ```  Ensure `True` is returned.
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: Enabling DDoS Network Protection on the virtual network, as described in the recommendation 'Ensure Azure DDoS Network Protection is Enabled on Virtual Networks', also satisfies this recommendation for the public IP addresses in that network whose protection mode is not `Disabled`. Azure DDoS Protection does not support public IP addresses attached to a NAT gateway, multitenant platform services, Azure Virtual WAN, or virtual machines in classic deployments. No built-in Azure Policy definition evaluates DDoS protection on public IP addresses.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, the protection mode is `VirtualNetworkInherited` or not set, so an address is protected only when its virtual network has DDoS Network Protection enabled.

Requirements.Description: Ensure Azure DDoS Network Protection is Enabled on Virtual Networks

Attributes.Description: Azure DDoS Network Protection defends resources in virtual networks against distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Public IP addresses in an unprotected virtual network are exposed to volumetric, protocol, and resource-exhaustion DDoS attacks that can take hosted workloads offline. Network Protection tunes mitigation to the traffic profile of each protected public IP address and adds attack analytics and DDoS Rapid Response access during an attack.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Network Protection is a fixed monthly plan for 100 public IP resources, charged per resource beyond that; one plan serves a tenant's subscriptions. DDoS IP Protection protects individual public IP addresses rather than the virtual network, so it does not satisfy this recommendation. It is cheaper below 15 public IPs but lacks rapid response, cost protection, and WAF discounts.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Virtual networks`. 2. Click the name of a virtual network. 3. Under `Settings`, click `DDoS protection`. 4. Next to `DDoS Network Protection`, click `Enable`. 5. Provide a DDoS protection plan resource ID, or select a DDoS protection plan from the drop-down menu. 6. Click `Save`. 7. Repeat steps 1-6 for each virtual network requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each virtual network requiring remediation, run the following command to enable DDoS protection:  ``` az network vnet update --resource-group <resource-group> --name <virtual-network> --ddos-protection true --ddos-protection-plan <ddos-protection-plan> ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each virtual network requiring remediation, run the following commands to enable DDoS protection:  ``` $vnet = Get-AzVirtualNetwork -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <virtual-network> $vnet.DdosProtectionPlan = New-Object Microsoft.Azure.Commands.Network.Models.PSResourceId $vnet.DdosProtectionPlan.Id = '<ddos-protection-plan-id>' $vnet.EnableDdosProtection = $true $vnet | Set-AzVirtualNetwork ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Virtual networks`. 2. Click the name of a virtual network. 3. Under `Settings`, click `DDoS protection`. 4. Ensure `DDoS Network Protection` is set to `Enable`. 5. Repeat steps 1-4 for each virtual network.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list the DDoS protection setting of every virtual network:  ``` az network vnet list --query "[].{Name:name, ResourceGroup:resourceGroup, EnableDdosProtection:enableDdosProtection}" --output table ```  Ensure `true` is returned for every virtual network.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Run the following command to list the DDoS protection setting of every virtual network:  ``` Get-AzVirtualNetwork | Select-Object Name, ResourceGroupName, EnableDdosProtection ```  Ensure `True` is returned for every virtual network.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [a7aca53f-2ed4-4466-a25e-0b45ade68efd](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2Fa7aca53f-2ed4-4466-a25e-0b45ade68efd) **- Name:** 'Azure DDoS Protection should be enabled'  **Note:** This Policy relies on a Microsoft Defender for Cloud assessment and treats virtual networks that assessment marks `NotApplicable` as compliant, so use the Azure Portal, Azure CLI, or PowerShell method for a definitive check.
Attributes.DefaultValue: DDoS protection is disabled by default.

Requirements.Description: Ensure That Soft Delete for Blobs on Azure Blob Storage Storage Accounts is Enabled

Attributes.Description: Blob soft delete keeps deleted blobs, snapshots, and versions recoverable for 1 to 365 days, and also keeps overwritten blobs on accounts without a hierarchical namespace. It is enabled or disabled per storage account with the Blob service; the compliant state is enabled with at least 7 days of retention.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Without soft delete or blob versioning, a deleted or overwritten blob is lost at once and the storage account cannot restore it. A user error, a faulty application, or an attacker with delete rights can therefore destroy blob data immediately, and the loss is permanent unless a separate backup exists.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Soft-deleted data is billed as active data until retention ends, so overwrite-heavy workloads cost more. On an account without a hierarchical namespace, blob soft delete blocks the Data Lake Storage (DFS) endpoint, so DFS clients must use the Blob endpoint, and it blocks upgrading to a hierarchical namespace until soft delete is off and all soft-deleted blobs have expired.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Storage accounts`. 2. Click on a storage account. 3. Under `Data management`, click `Data protection`. 4. Select `Turn on soft delete for blobs` (`Enable soft delete for blobs` on accounts with a hierarchical namespace). 5. Enter a retention period of 7 days or more. 6. Click `Save`. 7. Repeat steps 1-6 for each storage account requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each storage account requiring remediation (any account whose `kind` is not `FileStorage`), run the following command, setting `<retention-days>` to 7 or more:  ``` az storage account blob-service-properties update --account-name <storage-account> --resource-group <resource-group> --enable-delete-retention true --delete-retention-days <retention-days> ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each storage account requiring remediation (any account whose `Kind` is not `FileStorage`), run the following command, setting `<retention-days>` to 7 or more:  ``` Enable-AzStorageBlobDeleteRetentionPolicy -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -StorageAccountName <storage-account> -RetentionDays <retention-days> ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Note:** No built-in Azure Policy definition audits this setting; the built-in 'Configure soft delete for blobs and containers on Storage Accounts' deploys it instead and also requires container soft delete.  **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Storage accounts`. 2. Click on a storage account. 3. Under `Data management`, click `Data protection`. 4. Ensure that `Turn on soft delete for blobs` (`Enable soft delete for blobs` on accounts with a hierarchical namespace) is selected and the retention period is 7 days or more. 5. Repeat steps 1-4 for each storage account with the Blob service (every account except premium file share accounts).  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list each storage account and its kind:  ``` az storage account list --query "[].{name:name, resourceGroup:resourceGroup, kind:kind}" --output table ```  For each storage account whose `kind` is not `FileStorage`, run the following command:  ``` az storage account blob-service-properties show --account-name <storage-account> --resource-group <resource-group> --query deleteRetentionPolicy ```  Ensure that `enabled` is `true` and `days` is 7 or more; any other result is non-compliant.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Run the following command to list each storage account and its kind:  ``` Get-AzStorageAccount | Select-Object StorageAccountName, ResourceGroupName, Kind ```  For each storage account whose `Kind` is not `FileStorage`, run the following command:  ``` (Get-AzStorageBlobServiceProperty -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -StorageAccountName <storage-account>).DeleteRetentionPolicy ```  Ensure that `Enabled` is `True` and `Days` is 7 or more; any other result is non-compliant.
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: Blob soft delete does not recover a deleted container or a deleted storage account; those cases need container soft delete or Azure Backup.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, blob soft delete is enabled on accounts created in the Azure Portal and disabled on accounts created with the Azure CLI or PowerShell.

Requirements.Description: Ensure that 'Public Network Access' is 'Disabled' for Storage Accounts

Attributes.Description: Disable public network access to prevent exposure to the internet and reduce the risk of unauthorized access. Use private endpoints to securely manage access within trusted networks.  Disallowing public network access for a storage account overrides the public access settings for individual containers in that storage account.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: Disabling public network access improves security by ensuring that a storage account is not exposed on the public internet.  The default network configuration for a storage account permits a user with appropriate permissions to configure public network access to containers and blobs in a storage account. Keep in mind that public access to a container is always turned off by default and must be explicitly configured to permit anonymous requests. It grants read-only access to these resources without sharing the account key, and without requiring a shared access signature. It is recommended not to provide public network access to storage accounts until, and unless, it is strongly desired. A shared access signature token or Azure AD RBAC should be used for providing controlled and timed access to blob containers.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: **NOTE:** Prior to disabling public network access, it is strongly recommended that, for each storage account, either:  - virtual network integration is completed  OR  - private endpoints/links are set up as described in **"Ensure Private Endpoints are used to access Storage Accounts."**  Disabling public network access restricts direct access to the service. This enhances security but will require the configuration of a virtual network and/or private endpoints for any services or users needing access within trusted networks.  Access will have to be managed using shared access signatures or via Azure AD RBAC.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Remediate from Azure Portal**  First, follow Microsoft documentation and create shared access signature tokens for your blob containers. Then,  1. Go to `Storage Accounts`. 2. For each storage account, under the `Security + networking` section, click `Networking`. 3. Set `Public network access` to `Disabled`. 4. Click `Save`.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  Set 'Public Network Access' to `Disabled` on the storage account  ``` az storage account update --name <storage-account> --resource-group <resource-group> --public-network-access Disabled ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each Storage Account, run the following to set the `PublicNetworkAccess` setting to `Disabled`  ``` Set-AzStorageAccount -ResourceGroupName <resource group name> -Name <storage account name> -PublicNetworkAccess Disabled ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Storage Accounts`. 2. For each storage account, under the `Security + networking` section, click `Networking`. 3. Ensure the `Public network access` setting is set to `Disabled`.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Ensure `publicNetworkAccess` is `Disabled`  ``` az storage account show --name <storage-account> --resource-group <resource-group> --query "{publicNetworkAccess:publicNetworkAccess}" ```  **Audit from PowerShell**  For each Storage Account, ensure `PublicNetworkAccess` is `Disabled`  ``` Get-AzStorageAccount -Name <storage account name> -ResourceGroupName <resource group name> |select PublicNetworkAccess ```  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [b2982f36-99f2-4db5-8eff-283140c09693](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2Fb2982f36-99f2-4db5-8eff-283140c09693) **- Name:** 'Storage accounts should disable public network access'
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: This recommendation is based on the Common Reference Recommendation `Ensure public network access is Disabled`, from the `Common Reference Recommendations > Networking > Virtual Networks (VNets)` section.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, `Public Network Access` is set to `Enabled from all networks` for the Storage Account.

Requirements.Description: Ensure Default Network Access Rule for Storage Accounts is Set to Deny

Attributes.Description: Restricting default network access helps to provide a new layer of security, since storage accounts accept connections from clients on any network. To limit access to selected networks, the default action must be changed.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: **Note:** This recommendation is only applicable if Public Network Access has not been disabled due to necessity or exception.  Storage accounts should be configured to deny access to traffic from all networks (including internet traffic). Access can be granted to traffic from specific Azure Virtual networks, allowing a secure network boundary for specific applications to be built. Access can also be granted to public internet IP address ranges to enable connections from specific internet or on-premises clients. When network rules are configured, only applications from allowed networks can access a storage account. When calling from an allowed network, applications continue to require proper authorization (a valid access key or SAS token) to access the storage account.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: All allowed networks must be added to the allow list on each storage account, creating administrative overhead. This may result in loss of network connectivity, so do not enable it for critical resources during business hours without first confirming the required networks are permitted. Where access is enabled from selected networks, avoid adding public internet IP address ranges beyond those strictly required, as broad public allow entries weaken the intended restriction.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Navigate to `Storage accounts`. 2. Select the storage account to remediate. 3. In the service menu, under `Security + networking`, select `Networking`. 4. Select `Manage`. 5. Select `Enable`, then select `Enabled from selected networks`. 6. Add the virtual networks, IP address ranges, or resource instances that require access. 7. Select `Save`. 8.  9. Repeat for each storage account requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  Add an allow rule for each network that requires access before changing the default action, or connectivity to the account will be interrupted:  ``` az storage account network-rule add --resource-group <resource-group> --account-name <storage-account> --subnet <subnet-resource-id> ```  Then set the default network action to `Deny`:  ``` az storage account update --name <storage-account> --resource-group <resource-group> --default-action Deny ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  Add an allow rule for each network that requires access before changing the default action, or connectivity to the account will be interrupted:  ``` Add-AzStorageAccountNetworkRule -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <storage-account> -VirtualNetworkResourceId <subnet-resource-id> ```  Then set the default network action to `Deny`:  ``` Update-AzStorageAccountNetworkRuleSet -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <storage-account> -DefaultAction Deny ```  **Note:** Setting `Public network access` to `Disabled` (with access provided through private endpoints), or securing the account with a network security perimeter, restricts public access at least as strongly as the default-deny rule this recommendation configures. A network security perimeter supports HTTPS-based storage operations only; NFS, SMB, and SFTP access is blocked while the perimeter is in Enforced mode.
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Navigate to `Storage accounts`. 2. Select the storage account to review. 3. In the service menu, under `Security + networking`, select `Networking`. 4. Confirm `Public network access` is not set to `Enabled from all networks`. `Enabled from selected networks` (with the default rule denying unlisted traffic), `Disabled`, and `Secured by perimeter` are compliant states; `Enabled from all networks` is non-compliant. 5. Repeat for each storage account.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  To review every storage account in the subscription in one call, run the following command:  ``` az storage account list --query "[].{name:name, resourceGroup:resourceGroup, publicNetworkAccess:publicNetworkAccess, defaultAction:networkRuleSet.defaultAction}" --output table ```  To confirm a single storage account, run:  ``` az storage account show --name <storage-account> --resource-group <resource-group> --query "{publicNetworkAccess:publicNetworkAccess, defaultAction:networkRuleSet.defaultAction}" ```  An account whose publicNetworkAccess is `Disabled` or `SecuredByPerimeter` restricts public access regardless of the default rule and is compliant. An account whose publicNetworkAccess is `Enabled` (or empty, which is equivalent to `Enabled`) is compliant only when defaultAction is `Deny`; a defaultAction of `Allow` on such an account is non-compliant.  **Note:** Disabling public network access does not change the stored default rule, so an account with public access disabled may still report a defaultAction of `Allow`. Evaluate the two properties together as stated above.  **Audit from PowerShell**  ``` Get-AzStorageAccount -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <storage-account> | Select-Object PublicNetworkAccess, @{Name="DefaultAction";Expression={$_.NetworkRuleSet.DefaultAction}} ```  Apply the same evaluation: a PublicNetworkAccess of `Disabled` or `SecuredByPerimeter` is compliant; a PublicNetworkAccess of `Enabled` (or empty) requires a DefaultAction of `Deny`, and `Allow` is non-compliant.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [34c877ad-507e-4c82-993e-3452a6e0ad3c](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2F34c877ad-507e-4c82-993e-3452a6e0ad3c) **- Name:** 'Storage accounts should restrict network access' - **Policy ID:** [2a1a9cdf-e04d-429a-8416-3bfb72a1b26f](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2F2a1a9cdf-e04d-429a-8416-3bfb72a1b26f) **- Name:** 'Storage accounts should restrict network access using virtual network rules'  **Note:** The second Policy is a stricter, virtual-network-only variant: in addition to the default rule, it flags accounts that use IP-based allow rules, which this recommendation otherwise permits.
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: This recommendation is based on the Common Reference Recommendation `Ensure Network Access Rules are set to Deny-by-default`, from the `Common Reference Recommendations > Networking > Virtual Networks (VNets)` section.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, Storage Accounts will accept connections from clients on any network.

Requirements.Description: Ensure that 'Default to Microsoft Entra authorization in the Azure portal' is Set to 'Enabled'

Attributes.Description: The Azure portal authorizes access to blob, file share, and queue data with either the account access key or the signed-in user's Microsoft Entra account. The `Default to Microsoft Entra authorization in the Azure portal` setting, `Enabled` or `Disabled`, selects whether the portal uses Microsoft Entra ID by default.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: When the setting is not enabled, the portal accesses data with the account access key for any user whose role can list keys, such as Contributor. That access grants full read, write, and delete on all blob, file share, and queue data, bypasses data-access role assignments and conditions, and is logged as Shared Key authorization, not under the user's identity.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Portal users see no data without a data-access role: Storage Blob Data Reader or Storage Blob Data Contributor (blobs), Storage Queue Data Reader or Storage Queue Data Contributor (queues), or Storage File Data Privileged Reader or Storage File Data Privileged Contributor (file shares). Users who hold only a data-access role also need the Reader role on the storage account.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Note:** The Az.Storage storage account cmdlets do not expose this setting, so no PowerShell method is given.  **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Storage accounts`. 2. Click the name of a storage account. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Configuration`. 4. Set `Default to Microsoft Entra authorization in the Azure portal` to `Enabled`. 5. Click `Save`. 6. Repeat steps 1-5 for each storage account requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each storage account requiring remediation, run the following command:  ``` az storage account update --resource-group <resource-group> --name <storage-account> --set defaultToOAuthAuthentication=true ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Note:** No built-in Azure Policy definition audits this setting, and the Az.Storage storage account cmdlets do not expose it, so no Azure Policy or PowerShell method is given.  **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Storage accounts`. 2. Click the name of a storage account. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Configuration`. 4. Ensure that `Default to Microsoft Entra authorization in the Azure portal` is set to `Enabled`. 5. Repeat steps 1-4 for each storage account.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list the storage accounts where `defaultToOAuthAuthentication` is not `true`, including accounts where it is not set:  ``` az storage account list --query "[?defaultToOAuthAuthentication!=\`true\`].{name:name, resourceGroup:resourceGroup}" --output table ```  Ensure that no storage accounts are returned. Repeat for each subscription.
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: This setting changes only the portal's default, so a user who can list keys can still use the key; it does not disable Shared Key authorization. The recommendation "Ensure 'Allow storage account key access' for Azure Storage Accounts is 'Disabled'", in the Storage Accounts section of the CIS Microsoft Azure Storage Services Benchmark, does that. When `Allow storage account key access` is `Disabled`, the portal cannot use the key; the audit still requires this setting so the portal already defaults to Microsoft Entra ID if key access is re-enabled.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, `defaultToOAuthAuthentication` is not set and is interpreted as `false`.

Requirements.Description: Ensure that 'Secure transfer required' is Set to 'Enabled'

Attributes.Description: A storage account either accepts requests over insecure connections or rejects them. The `Secure transfer required` setting is `Enabled` or `Disabled`; when `Enabled`, it rejects REST API requests over HTTP and, unless a per-protocol encryption-in-transit setting is enabled, unencrypted SMB and NFS connections to Azure file shares.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: With secure transfer disabled, REST requests to the account can travel over plain HTTP. Data, shared access signature tokens, and request headers then cross the network unencrypted, where they can be read or modified in transit.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Clients that call the REST API over HTTP fail once secure transfer is required. SMB connections without encryption, such as SMB 2.1, and NFS file shares mounted without the AZNFS mount helper also fail.  For Azure Files, when `Require encryption in transit` is enabled for SMB or NFS, `Secure transfer required` applies only to REST traffic for the account's file shares, and the per-protocol setting governs that protocol. A custom domain mapped directly to a blob endpoint serves HTTP only, so on an account that requires secure transfer, serve the custom domain over HTTPS through Azure Front Door or another HTTPS-fronting service, such as Azure CDN.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Storage accounts`. 2. Click on a storage account. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Configuration`. 4. Set `Secure transfer required` to `Enabled`. 5. Click `Save`. 6. Repeat steps 1-5 for each storage account requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each storage account requiring remediation, run the following command:  ``` az storage account update --resource-group <resource-group> --name <storage-account> --https-only true ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each storage account requiring remediation, run the following command:  ``` Set-AzStorageAccount -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <storage-account> -EnableHttpsTrafficOnly $true ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Storage accounts`. 2. Click on a storage account. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Configuration`. 4. Ensure that `Secure transfer required` is set to `Enabled`. 5. Repeat steps 1-4 for each storage account.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list each storage account and its secure transfer setting:  ``` az storage account list --query "[].{name:name, resourceGroup:resourceGroup, enableHttpsTrafficOnly:enableHttpsTrafficOnly}" --output table ```  Ensure that `enableHttpsTrafficOnly` is `true` for each storage account.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Run the following command to list each storage account and its secure transfer setting:  ``` Get-AzStorageAccount | Select-Object StorageAccountName, ResourceGroupName, EnableHttpsTrafficOnly ```  Ensure that `EnableHttpsTrafficOnly` is `True` for each storage account.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [404c3081-a854-4457-ae30-26a93ef643f9](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2F404c3081-a854-4457-ae30-26a93ef643f9) **- Name:** 'Secure transfer to storage accounts should be enabled'
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, `Secure transfer required` is `Enabled` on storage accounts created with API version 2019-04-01 or later.

Requirements.Description: Ensure the 'Minimum TLS version' for Storage Accounts is Set to 'Version 1.2'

Attributes.Description: A storage account's `Minimum TLS version` setting defines the lowest Transport Layer Security (TLS) version it accepts for requests, and it is either set to a version or left unset. The compliant value is `Version 1.2`.  **Warning:** Azure Storage stopped supporting TLS 1.0 and 1.1 for all storage accounts on February 3, 2026, so requests that use those versions fail regardless of this setting.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 have known weaknesses and lack modern cipher suites. An account without an explicit `Version 1.2` minimum relies on platform behavior, not its own configuration, so a future platform or configuration change could again permit those protocols. An explicit floor guards against that change and is the only state audits and Azure Policy can verify at scale.  **POST-QUANTUM CRYPTOGRAPHY:** TLS v1.3 introduces cryptographic suites which make Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) algorithms accessible. Where possible, TLS v1.3 should be implemented as the sole protocol in use for the security of data in transit, but only if TLS 1.2 interoperability is not required.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Because Azure Storage has rejected TLS 1.0 and 1.1 requests since February 3, 2026, setting the minimum to `Version 1.2` does not block any client that can currently connect.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Storage accounts`. 2. Click on a storage account. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Configuration`. 4. Set `Minimum TLS version` to `Version 1.2`. 5. Click `Save`. 6. Repeat steps 1-5 for each storage account requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each storage account requiring remediation, run the following command:  ``` az storage account update --resource-group <resource-group> --name <storage-account> --min-tls-version TLS1_2 ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each storage account requiring remediation, run the following command:  ``` Set-AzStorageAccount -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <storage-account> -MinimumTlsVersion TLS1_2 ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Storage accounts`. 2. Click on a storage account. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Configuration`. 4. Ensure that `Minimum TLS version` is set to `Version 1.2`. 5. Repeat steps 1-4 for each storage account.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list each storage account and its minimum TLS version:  ``` az storage account list --query "[].{name:name, resourceGroup:resourceGroup, minimumTlsVersion:minimumTlsVersion}" --output table ```  Ensure that `minimumTlsVersion` is `TLS1_2` for each storage account. An empty value (not set) or any other value is non-compliant.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Run the following command to list each storage account and its minimum TLS version:  ``` Get-AzStorageAccount | Select-Object StorageAccountName, ResourceGroupName, MinimumTlsVersion ```  Ensure that `MinimumTlsVersion` is `TLS1_2` for each storage account. An empty value (not set) or any other value is non-compliant.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [fe83a0eb-a853-422d-aac2-1bffd182c5d0](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2Ffe83a0eb-a853-422d-aac2-1bffd182c5d0) **- Name:** 'Storage accounts should have the specified minimum TLS version'  Assign this policy with the `minimumTlsVersion` parameter set to `TLS1_2`.
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: Azure Storage also accepts TLS 1.3, which clients negotiate automatically when available, but TLS 1.3 cannot be set as the minimum version. Since the February 3, 2026 retirement, the platform rejects TLS 1.0 and 1.1 whatever this setting holds; this overrides the unset-property behavior described in Microsoft's minimum TLS version configuration article, which says an account with no minimum set accepts TLS 1.0 or later.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, the Azure Portal sets `Version 1.2`; the Azure CLI, PowerShell, and templates leave the setting unset.

Requirements.Description: Ensure that 'Allow Blob anonymous access' is Set to 'Disabled'

Attributes.Description: A storage account either allows or disallows anonymous read access to its blob data. The `Allow Blob anonymous access` setting selects between `Enabled` and `Disabled`; when `Disabled`, it overrides the anonymous access level of every container in the account.
Attributes.RationaleStatement: With anonymous access allowed on the account, any user who can change a container's access level can expose that container publicly. Anyone can then read its blobs without credentials, and a container set to the Container level can also be listed, so its contents can be enumerated and copied with no identity attached to the requests.
Attributes.ImpactStatement: Once anonymous access is disabled, anonymous requests to every container in the account fail, including containers already set for anonymous access. A static website's content stays publicly readable through the static website endpoint.
Attributes.RemediationProcedure: **Remediate from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Storage accounts`. 2. Click on a storage account. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Configuration`. 4. Set `Allow Blob anonymous access` to `Disabled`. 5. Click `Save`. 6. Repeat steps 1-5 for each storage account requiring remediation.  **Remediate from Azure CLI**  For each storage account requiring remediation, run the following command:  ``` az storage account update --resource-group <resource-group> --name <storage-account> --allow-blob-public-access false ```  **Remediate from PowerShell**  For each storage account requiring remediation, run the following command:  ``` Set-AzStorageAccount -ResourceGroupName <resource-group> -Name <storage-account> -AllowBlobPublicAccess $false ```
Attributes.AuditProcedure: **Audit from Azure Portal**  1. Go to `Storage accounts`. 2. Click on a storage account. 3. Under `Settings`, click `Configuration`. 4. Ensure that `Allow Blob anonymous access` is set to `Disabled`. 5. Repeat steps 1-4 for each storage account.  **Audit from Azure CLI**  Run the following command to list each storage account and its anonymous access setting:  ``` az storage account list --query "[].{name:name, resourceGroup:resourceGroup, allowBlobPublicAccess:allowBlobPublicAccess}" --output table ```  Ensure that `allowBlobPublicAccess` is `false` for each storage account. A value of `true`, or an empty value (not set), is non-compliant.  **Audit from PowerShell**  Run the following command to list each storage account and its anonymous access setting:  ``` Get-AzStorageAccount | Select-Object StorageAccountName, ResourceGroupName, AllowBlobPublicAccess ```  Ensure that `AllowBlobPublicAccess` is `False` for each storage account. A value of `True`, or an empty value (not set), is non-compliant.  **Audit from Azure Policy**  If referencing a digital copy of this Benchmark, clicking a Policy ID will open a link to the associated Policy definition in Azure.  If referencing a printed copy, you can search Policy IDs from this URL: https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyMenuBlade/~/Definitions  - **Policy ID:** [4fa4b6c0-31ca-4c0d-b10d-24b96f62a751](https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_Policy/PolicyDetailBlade/definitionId/%2Fproviders%2FMicrosoft.Authorization%2FpolicyDefinitions%2F4fa4b6c0-31ca-4c0d-b10d-24b96f62a751) **- Name:** 'Storage account public access should be disallowed'
Attributes.AdditionalInformation: Microsoft advises moving data that must stay publicly readable to a separate storage account reserved for anonymous access and holding no sensitive data; such an account fails this recommendation's audit and should be recorded as a documented exception. The cited Azure Policy excludes storage accounts managed by Azure Red Hat OpenShift (accounts named `cluster*` or `imageregistry*` in resource groups whose names begin with `aro-`), so its results for those accounts can differ from the Azure CLI and PowerShell audits.
Attributes.DefaultValue: By default, anonymous access is disallowed, but the `allowBlobPublicAccess` property may be unset rather than `false`; this recommendation's audit treats an unset value as non-compliant.
